subject: CI/CD Pipelines
summary: CI/CD is the machinery that turns a commit into running production software, and it is the one system that touches every part of an organisation's engineering practice: source control, build reproducibility, test strategy, artifact management, cloud credentials, and the release itself. Interviewers probe it because a candidate's pipeline answers reveal how they actually work — whether they understand that CI is about merge frequency rather than a tool, whether they build once and promote an immutable artifact or silently ship an untested rebuild, whether they can make a deploy safe with canaries and flags and reverse it when it is not, and whether they know that a pipeline holding every environment's credentials is the highest-value target in the company. This subject covers the practices and their mechanisms: pipeline stages and the feedback-loop budget, GitHub Actions, Jenkins, and GitLab CI at the level of what actually executes where, caching and container-build performance, matrix builds and sharding, secrets and OIDC workload identity, deployment strategies and rollback, database migrations under continuous delivery, and supply-chain security.

sections.title: 1. CI vs Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment: Three Different Claims
sections.content:
These three terms get used interchangeably in job descriptions and almost never in interviews. An interviewer asking "what's the difference?" is checking whether you understand that each is a *practice* with a testable definition, not a product you install.

**Continuous Integration** is a claim about how often code is merged into the shared mainline. The original definition is that every developer integrates their work into trunk at least once a day, and that each integration is verified by an automated build and test run. The point is economic: the cost of merging two branches grows superlinearly with how long they have diverged, because conflicts are not just textual but semantic — I renamed the method you added three callers to. If you integrate hourly you pay a tiny cost constantly; if you integrate after three weeks you pay a large, unpredictable, and un-schedulable cost all at once. The automated build exists to make integration *safe* to do that often. This is why "we have Jenkins" is not the same as "we do CI." A team with fifteen long-lived feature branches that each run a full test suite is doing continuous *building*, not continuous integration — they have automated the verification of divergence rather than removing it. The practice that actually delivers CI is trunk-based development: short-lived branches (hours to a day or two), merged behind feature flags if the work is incomplete.

**Continuous Delivery** is a claim about the artifact. Every commit that passes the pipeline produces a release candidate that is *provably deployable* — built, tested, packaged, and sitting in an artifact repository — and the pipeline has a working, rehearsed path to push it to production. The decision to actually release is a business decision made by a human pressing a button. The test of whether you have continuous delivery is not "can you deploy" but "is your software always in a releasable state, and is deploying a non-event?" If shipping requires a code freeze, a release branch that gets stabilised for two weeks, and a Saturday night maintenance window, you do not have it.

**Continuous Deployment** removes the human button. Every commit that goes green in the pipeline is deployed to production automatically. This is a strict superset of continuous delivery and requires much more: high-confidence automated tests, progressive rollout with automated metric gates, fast automatic rollback, and feature flags so that "deployed" and "released to users" are decoupled. Most large organisations run continuous delivery to production for some services and continuous deployment for others; almost nobody runs continuous deployment for a database schema or a mobile app binary, since the app store review step makes it structurally impossible.

The useful mental model for an interview: CI is about the *merge*, continuous delivery is about the *artifact*, continuous deployment is about the *release*. And the way the industry measures whether any of this works is the four DORA metrics — deployment frequency, lead time for changes (commit to running in production), change failure rate, and failed-deployment recovery time. Those four are deliberately paired: two measure speed, two measure stability, and the research finding that made them famous is that the two do not trade off against each other. Teams that deploy more often tend to have *lower* change failure rates, because small changes are easier to review, test, and reason about when they break. If you only remember one line for the interview: batch size is the hidden variable behind every one of these metrics.

# A concrete test of which one you actually have.

CI:
  git log --format='%ci' origin/main | head -50   # are commits landing on trunk daily?
  git branch -r --sort=-committerdate             # any branch older than ~2 days?
  # If feature branches live for weeks, you do not have CI, whatever the tool says.

Continuous Delivery:
  # Pick the newest green commit on main. Can you answer these in under a minute?
  #  - Where is its build artifact? (immutable, addressable, retrievable)
  #  - What is the one command that puts it in production?
  #  - When was that command last run successfully? (if > 1 week: it is not rehearsed)

Continuous Deployment:
  # No human in the path between "tests green" and "serving traffic".
  # Requires: progressive rollout + automated metric gate + automated rollback.

DORA four keys (what to instrument):
  deployment_frequency    = count(prod deploys) / time
  lead_time_for_changes   = p50(deploy_time - first_commit_time_of_that_change)
  change_failure_rate     = deploys causing incident/rollback / total deploys
  failed_deploy_recovery  = p50(time from bad deploy detected -> service restored)

sections.title: 2. Anatomy of a Deployment Pipeline: Stages, Gates, and the Ten-Minute Budget
sections.content:
A deployment pipeline is a directed acyclic graph of automated stages that a commit must traverse to reach production, where each stage is an increasingly expensive and increasingly production-like test of the *same artifact*. Two properties define it: the artifact is built exactly once at the head of the pipeline, and every subsequent stage either passes it forward or kills it. If any stage rebuilds from source, you have broken the chain of evidence — you are now testing something other than what you will deploy.

The canonical shape:

```
  commit
    |
  [ COMMIT STAGE ]  compile + unit tests + lint + static analysis   (<10 min)
    |               produces ONE immutable artifact -> registry
    +----------------+----------------+----------------+
    |                |                |                |
 [integration]  [contract tests]  [SAST/deps]   [container scan]     (parallel)
    +----------------+----------------+----------------+
    |
  [ DEPLOY staging ] real infra, real config mechanism
    |
  [ smoke + acceptance + perf ]
    |
  [ manual gate / approval ]     <- continuous delivery stops here
    |                               continuous deployment does not
  [ PROGRESSIVE PROD ROLLOUT ] canary -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%, metric-gated
```

The **commit stage** is the one with a hard budget, and it is the single most important operational number in your CI system. The widely used target is ten minutes. The reason is behavioural, not technical: if feedback takes longer than the time a developer will sit and wait, they context-switch to another task, and the cost of a broken build multiplies — by the time the red build is noticed, three more commits have landed on top of it and nobody knows which one broke it. Beyond about ten minutes people also start batching pushes, which directly attacks the CI premise. So the commit stage gets only the fast, deterministic, high-value checks: compile, unit tests, linting, type checking. Anything requiring a database, a network, or a browser goes downstream.

**Fail fast, and order by cost-to-signal ratio.** Within the commit stage, run the checks that fail most often and cheapest first. Compile before test. Lint before compile if lint is faster. Do not spend 90 seconds of test time to discover a missing import. Some teams run a tiny smoke subset of tests first, purely to catch catastrophic breakage before committing the whole runner fleet.

**Fan out downstream.** Integration tests, security scanning, dependency auditing, and container image scanning have no dependency on each other, so they run in parallel against the artifact from the commit stage. Their combined wall-clock time is the slowest one, not the sum. This is what GitHub Actions `needs`, GitLab `needs`, and Jenkins `parallel` are for.

**Gates are policy, not tests.** A gate is a stage that requires something other than a passing test: a human approval, a change-management ticket, a time window, a required reviewer on a protected environment. Encode them in the pipeline (GitHub Environments with required reviewers, GitLab `when: manual` on a protected environment, Jenkins `input`) rather than in a wiki, because an un-encoded gate is a gate that gets skipped under pressure — and a gate that lives only in someone's head produces no audit trail when the auditor asks who approved the change.

**Separate the pipeline's success criteria from the tests' success criteria.** Not every check should block. Security scanners with a high false-positive rate, performance benchmarks with noisy baselines, and new linters being rolled out should start as advisory (`allow_failure: true` in GitLab, `continue-on-error: true` in Actions) and be promoted to blocking only once their false-positive rate is low enough that people stop ignoring them. A pipeline that cries wolf gets bypassed with `--no-verify` and admin merges, and then you have no pipeline at all.

The production failure mode worth naming in an interview: **pipelines that grow without a budget**. Every incident adds a check, no one ever removes one, and eighteen months later the commit stage takes 47 minutes, developers push once a day in a batch, and the pipeline that was supposed to enable CI is now the thing preventing it. Treat commit-stage p95 duration as an SLO with a named owner, and review it like any other SLO.

# GitHub Actions: the shape above, expressed as a DAG.
name: pipeline
on: [push, pull_request]

concurrency:                       # kill superseded runs on the same ref
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

permissions:
  contents: read                   # least privilege by default

jobs:
  commit-stage:                    # <-- the 10-minute budget lives here
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 12            # a budget you do not enforce is a wish
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '20', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test -- --ci
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: app-dist
          path: dist/
          retention-days: 7

  integration:
    needs: commit-stage            # fan-out: these run concurrently
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test }
        ports: ['5432:5432']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: app-dist, path: dist/ }
      - run: npm ci && npm run test:integration

  security:
    needs: commit-stage
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm audit --audit-level=high

  deploy-staging:
    needs: [integration, security] # fan-in
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh staging

  deploy-prod:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production        # required reviewers configured on the env
    steps:                         # = the manual gate, enforced by the platform
      - run: ./deploy.sh production

sections.title: 3. Build Once, Promote Everywhere: Artifacts, Immutability, and Digests
sections.content:
The single most load-bearing rule in a deployment pipeline is: **build the artifact once, then promote that exact, byte-identical artifact through every environment.** Interviewers probe this because violating it is extremely common and the failure mode is nasty.

The anti-pattern looks reasonable. You have a `build-staging` job and a `build-prod` job; each checks out the tag and runs `docker build`. But `docker build` is not a pure function of your source tree. It resolves `FROM node:20` to whatever digest that tag points at *today*. It runs `apt-get install` against a mirror whose package versions moved. It runs `npm install` (not `npm ci`) and picks up a patch release published an hour ago. It bakes in a different build timestamp, a different `$HOME`, a different locale. The result is that the thing you tested in staging and the thing you deployed to production are two different binaries, and every hour of debugging you spend afterwards is spent on the wrong artifact. When you eventually find the difference, it is always something you could not have guessed.

Building once also gives you the property that makes rollback trivial: **the previous version still exists**. If deploying means "rebuild from tag v1.4.2", rolling back means rebuilding from v1.4.1, which takes eight minutes and may not even reproduce. If deploying means "point the deployment at `registry/app@sha256:abc...`", rolling back is a control-plane update that takes seconds and is guaranteed to produce the bits that were previously working.

**Tags are mutable; digests are not.** This is the mechanical detail that separates a strong answer from a vague one. A container image tag is a pointer in the registry's tag index; pushing `app:v1.4.2` a second time silently re-points it. A digest (`sha256:...`) is the content hash of the image manifest, so `app@sha256:...` is a name that can only ever refer to one artifact. Production deployment manifests should reference digests. Tags are fine as human-readable aliases for discovery and fine in a `FROM` line during development, but a release pipeline should resolve tag to digest once, early, and pass the digest downstream. The same logic applies to base images: `FROM node:20` means your "reproducible" build silently changes when Node ships 20.11.2. Pin the base image by digest for anything you ship.

**What promotion actually means.** Promotion is a metadata change, not a rebuild. Concretely: the artifact lives in one registry repository; a separate record — a Git commit in a config repo, a database row, an alias tag like `prod-current`, or an OCI attestation — says which digest each environment should run. Promoting from staging to production writes that record. This is the core idea of GitOps: the desired state of each environment is a Git commit referencing an immutable digest, so "what is in prod and who put it there" is answerable with `git log` rather than by asking around.

**Configuration is the thing that varies, not the artifact.** If the artifact is identical across environments, everything environment-specific must be injected at deploy or run time: environment variables, mounted config, a config service. The obvious violation is baking `API_URL=https://staging.example.com` into the build. The subtle violation is baking in a *build-time* feature flag, which makes the staging artifact behaviourally different from the production one — you have re-created the problem you were avoiding, just less visibly.

**Repository layout and retention.** Use one repository per artifact with immutable tags enabled where the registry supports it (ECR immutable tags, Artifactory/Nexus immutable repos, GitHub Packages retention rules). Artifacts accumulate fast: a 400 MB image produced 300 times a day is roughly 120 GB/day before layer sharing. You need a retention policy — but the policy must never delete an artifact that is currently deployed *or* is the last-known-good rollback target. "Delete images older than 30 days" has taken down production more than once by garbage-collecting the image a long-lived, digest-pinned deployment was still pulling on scale-out. The correct rule reads: keep the last N per branch, plus everything referenced by any live environment, plus everything tagged as a release, regardless of age.

# 1) Build once. Resolve to a DIGEST immediately and never mention the tag again.
IMAGE=ghcr.io/acme/api
GIT_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)

docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64 \
  --tag "$IMAGE:$GIT_SHA" \
  --provenance=true --sbom=true \
  --push .

# Read back the immutable digest the registry assigned.
DIGEST=$(docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE:$GIT_SHA" \
         --format '{{.Manifest.Digest}}')
echo "artifact=$IMAGE@$DIGEST"        # <- this string IS the release candidate

# 2) Promote = move a pointer, never rebuild.
#    Add an alias tag without re-uploading a single layer:
docker buildx imagetools create -t "$IMAGE:staging" "$IMAGE@$DIGEST"
docker buildx imagetools create -t "$IMAGE:prod"    "$IMAGE@$DIGEST"

# 3) Deploy by digest, not tag.
kubectl set image deploy/api api="$IMAGE@$DIGEST"
kubectl rollout status deploy/api --timeout=300s

# 4) Ask production what it is ACTUALLY running (tags lie, digests do not):
kubectl get pods -l app=api \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID}{"\n"}{end}' \
  | sort -u

# --- Dockerfile side: pin the base image by digest too, and build in stages ---
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim@sha256:<digest> AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12@sha256:<digest> AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
USER 1000
CMD ["dist/server.js"]

sections.title: 4. GitHub Actions: The Object Model and What Actually Executes Where
sections.content:
GitHub Actions has a four-level object model, and most confusion comes from not knowing which level owns which guarantee.

A **workflow** is a YAML file in `.github/workflows/`. It is triggered by `on:` — repository events (`push`, `pull_request`, `release`, `issue_comment`), schedules (`schedule: cron`), manual dispatch (`workflow_dispatch`), API dispatch (`repository_dispatch`), or being called by another workflow (`workflow_call`). One triggering event produces one run. The workflow owns run-level concerns: `concurrency`, default `permissions`, default `env`, and `defaults.run` (shell and working directory).

A **job** is the unit of scheduling and isolation. Every job gets its **own fresh runner** — a clean VM or container. Jobs in the same workflow run in parallel by default; `needs:` creates the dependency edges that turn the job set into a DAG. This is the single most important fact about the model: **jobs share no filesystem and no process state**. A file written in job A does not exist in job B. Anything crossing the job boundary must go through an explicit channel: `outputs` (small strings), artifacts (files), the cache (best-effort files), or an external system. Candidates who write a `build` job and a `test` job and then wonder why `./dist` is missing have not internalised this.

A **step** is a single unit of work inside a job, and steps *do* share the runner: same filesystem, same working directory, same user. A step is either `run:` (a shell command; the default shell on Linux runners is `bash` invoked with `-e`, so the step fails on the first non-zero exit) or `uses:` (an action). Each `run:` step is a *separate shell process*, so `export FOO=bar` in one step is invisible in the next — to persist an environment variable you append `FOO=bar` to the file at `$GITHUB_ENV`; to publish a value for later steps or downstream jobs, append `name=value` to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`. (The old `::set-output` workflow command is deprecated and disabled.)

An **action** is a reusable step implementation, referenced as `owner/repo@ref`, `./local/path`, or `docker://image`. Three flavours: JavaScript actions (run directly on the runner via Node — fastest, cross-platform), Docker container actions (Linux runners only; the action runs in a container with the workspace bind-mounted), and composite actions (a bundle of steps in YAML; each `run` step must declare `shell:`).

A **runner** is the machine executing a job. GitHub-hosted runners are **ephemeral**: a fresh VM per job, destroyed afterwards. That ephemerality is a security property (no state leaks between jobs; a compromised job cannot persist) and a performance cost (nothing is warm — hence caching). Self-hosted runners are yours, and by default they are *persistent*, which reverses both properties. The rule that matters: **never attach a persistent self-hosted runner to a public repository.** Anyone can open a pull request, and if fork PRs execute on that runner, that pull request is remote code execution on your machine with whatever credentials, cloud instance role, and network reachability it has. Use ephemeral runners (`--ephemeral`, or actions-runner-controller on Kubernetes) so each job gets a clean pod, and keep the runner's network access minimal.

Two more mechanics worth knowing. **Matrix** (`strategy.matrix`) is a job-level fan-out: the job template is instantiated once per combination, each on its own runner. **`if:`** conditions are evaluated by the runner service, and by default a step or job is skipped once something upstream has failed; `if: always()`, `if: failure()`, and `if: cancelled()` override that — this is how you attach "always upload the test report" and "notify on failure" steps. Note also that a skipped job counts as successful for a downstream `needs:`, which is a common source of a deploy job quietly running after its gate was skipped; guard with an explicit `if:` that checks `needs.<job>.result == 'success'` when that matters.

Defaults worth remembering: a job times out after 6 hours unless you set `timeout-minutes`, and a workflow run is bounded at 35 days. Both are far too generous — set `timeout-minutes` explicitly on every job so a hung test does not burn a runner for six hours.

name: ci
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths-ignore: ['docs/**', '**.md']       # monorepo: skip irrelevant changes
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        type: choice
        options: [staging, production]

permissions:
  contents: read                              # override the repo-wide default

env:
  NODE_ENV: test                              # workflow-level default

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}   # cross-job channel (strings)
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }              # default is a depth-1 shallow clone;
                                              # git describe / diff-vs-base need history
      - id: meta
        run: |
          VERSION="1.4.$(git rev-list --count HEAD)"
          echo "version=$VERSION" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"   # -> steps/jobs outputs
          echo "APP_VERSION=$VERSION" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"  # -> later STEPS' env

      - run: echo "building $APP_VERSION"     # visible: same job, later step

      - run: npm ci && npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4      # cross-job channel (files)
        with: { name: dist, path: dist/ }

      - name: Test report (runs even if tests failed)
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: junit, path: reports/ }

      - name: Render a summary panel on the run page
        run: |
          {
            echo "### Build ${APP_VERSION}"
            echo ""
            echo "| metric | value |"
            echo "|---|---|"
            echo "| bundle | $(du -sh dist | cut -f1) |"
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # FRESH runner: dist/ from the build job does NOT exist here until downloaded.
    # Also note: `needs` is satisfied by a SKIPPED job, so be explicit when it matters.
    if: needs.build.result == 'success'
    env:
      VERSION: ${{ needs.build.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: dist, path: dist/ }
      - run: ./deploy.sh "$VERSION"

sections.title: 5. GitHub Actions in Practice: Expressions, Reuse, Environments, Concurrency
sections.content:
Once you know the object model, the things that decide whether a GitHub Actions setup scales are expressions, reuse, and run-level control.

**Expressions and contexts.** `${{ }}` is evaluated by the Actions runner service *before* the step's shell ever starts — it is textual template substitution into the generated script. Available contexts include `github` (event payload, ref, sha, actor), `env`, `vars` (repo/org configuration variables — non-secret), `secrets`, `job`, `steps`, `runner`, `needs`, `matrix`, and `inputs`. Functions include `contains`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `format`, `join`, `toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `hashFiles`, and the status checks `success()`, `failure()`, `always()`, `cancelled()`. `fromJSON` is the escape hatch for dynamic matrices: a job emits a JSON array as an output, and a downstream job does `strategy: matrix: target: ${{ fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.targets) }}`. That is how you build a monorepo pipeline that only tests the services whose files changed.

The security consequence of "substitution happens before the shell runs" is **script injection**: never interpolate attacker-controllable strings (`github.event.pull_request.title`, branch names, issue bodies) directly into a `run:` block. Pass them through `env:` instead and reference them as shell variables, so the value is data rather than code. The pipeline-security section covers why in detail.

**Reusable workflows vs composite actions.** These solve different problems and interviewers like the distinction. A *composite action* packages a sequence of **steps** — it runs inside a caller's job, on the caller's runner, and cannot specify `runs-on`, a matrix, or multiple jobs. Use it for "the six steps we always run to set up the toolchain." A *reusable workflow* (`on: workflow_call`) packages whole **jobs** — the caller invokes it with `jobs.<id>.uses:` and it brings its own `runs-on`, its own matrix, its own job graph. Use it for "the standard build-test-scan-publish pipeline every service repo runs." Reusable workflows take typed `inputs`, explicit `secrets` (or `secrets: inherit`), and expose `outputs`; nesting is limited to four levels deep. One gotcha: a reusable workflow's jobs get their own `permissions`, and the caller can only grant permissions it already has — it cannot escalate.

**Environments** are the deployment-control primitive and are underused. An environment (`environment: production` on a job) can carry required reviewers (the job pauses until a human approves), a wait timer, a deployment branch policy (only `main` may deploy here), and environment-scoped secrets invisible to jobs targeting other environments. Crucially, the environment also appears in the OIDC token's `sub` claim, so a cloud IAM trust policy can be written to trust only jobs running against the `production` environment. That means a compromised feature branch cannot mint production credentials even though it can run workflows.

**Concurrency.** By default every push starts a run and they all execute. On an active repo this wastes enormous runner time — five pushes in ten minutes means four runs testing superseded code — and, worse, it allows two deploy jobs to run simultaneously against the same environment and interleave. `concurrency: { group: ..., cancel-in-progress: true }` keyed on `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` fixes PR runs. For deploys, use the *opposite* setting: a group keyed on the environment name with `cancel-in-progress: false`, so deploys queue and serialise rather than cancelling a half-finished rollout. Cancelling a deploy mid-`kubectl apply` is an excellent way to leave a cluster in a state nobody designed.

**Setup actions and caching.** The `setup-*` actions (`setup-node`, `setup-python`, `setup-java`, `setup-go`) accept a `cache:` input that wires up dependency caching with a key derived from your lockfile. Prefer that over hand-rolling `actions/cache` for the common case; hand-roll only when you need a non-standard path or key.

**Merge queues.** GitHub's merge queue solves the semantic-conflict problem that required status checks alone cannot: two PRs each green against `main`, but broken when both are merged. The queue builds speculative merge commits in order and tests each, evicting any PR that fails. If you run trunk-based development at any scale, this is the mechanism that keeps `main` green without serialising humans. Workflows opt in with the `merge_group` trigger.

# ---------- reusable workflow: .github/workflows/service-ci.yml ----------
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      service:   { required: true,  type: string }
      node:      { required: false, type: string, default: '20' }
    secrets:
      NPM_TOKEN: { required: false }
    outputs:
      digest:    { value: "${{ jobs.build.outputs.digest }}" }

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs: { digest: "${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}" }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: "${{ inputs.node }}", cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci && npm test
      - id: push
        run: echo "digest=$(./build-and-push.sh ${{ inputs.service }})" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

# ---------- caller ----------
jobs:
  api:
    uses: acme/ci-workflows/.github/workflows/service-ci.yml@v3
    with: { service: api }
    secrets: inherit

# ---------- dynamic matrix from changed paths (monorepo) ----------
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs: { services: "${{ steps.f.outputs.services }}" }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - id: f
        env:
          BASE: ${{ github.base_ref || 'main' }}
        run: |
          CHANGED=$(git diff --name-only "origin/$BASE...HEAD" \
                    | awk -F/ '/^services\//{print $2}' | sort -u | jq -R . | jq -sc .)
          echo "services=${CHANGED:-[]}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  test:
    needs: plan
    if: needs.plan.outputs.services != '[]'
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        service: ${{ fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.services) }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: make -C "services/${{ matrix.service }}" test

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

# deploy job/workflow:
concurrency:
  group: deploy-production        # not keyed on ref: one prod deploy at a time
  cancel-in-progress: false       # queue; never kill a rollout mid-flight

runs:
  using: composite

    - run: npm ci
      shell: bash                 # required in composite actions

sections.title: 6. Jenkins: Controller/Agent Architecture and the Declarative Pipeline
sections.content:
Jenkins is still the most common CI system in large enterprises, and interviews at those companies go straight to architecture and Jenkinsfile syntax.

**Architecture.** A Jenkins **controller** (formerly "master") holds configuration, job definitions, build history, the plugin set, and the web UI, and it *schedules* work. **Agents** (formerly "slaves") are separate machines or containers that actually execute build steps. An agent connects to the controller either inbound (the agent dials the controller — historically over JNLP, now typically WebSocket, which is the right choice when the agent sits behind NAT) or outbound (the controller SSHes into the agent). Each agent advertises a number of **executors** — concurrent build slots — and a set of **labels**. A pipeline's `agent { label 'linux && docker' }` is a label expression the scheduler matches against.

The first operational rule: **set the controller's executor count to zero.** If builds run on the controller, arbitrary pipeline code executes in the same JVM and filesystem as your credentials store, your job config, and `$JENKINS_HOME`. A single malicious or careless Jenkinsfile becomes full compromise. Related: the controller is a stateful single point of failure — `$JENKINS_HOME` *is* the system, so it must be backed up and restore-tested, and open-source Jenkins controllers are not clustered, so genuine HA is hard.

**Declarative vs scripted.** Jenkins pipelines are Groovy, but there are two dialects. *Scripted* pipelines are raw Groovy: `node('linux') { stage('build') { sh 'make' } }` — maximum flexibility, no structure, and Jenkins cannot validate or visualise them well. *Declarative* pipelines wrap a fixed schema around it: `pipeline { agent ... stages { ... } post { ... } }`. Declarative is what you should write and what interviewers expect. It gives you validation before the build starts, proper stage visualisation, `post` conditions, `options`, `when` guards, and `parallel` — and you can still drop into imperative Groovy inside a `script { }` block when the schema genuinely cannot express something. Reaching for `script { }` every third line is a signal you should be using a shared library instead.

**The directives you must know.** `agent` (at pipeline level, or per-stage to override; `agent none` at the top plus per-stage agents lets each stage pick its environment and avoids holding an executor during a manual `input`). `environment` for env vars and credentials binding. `options` for `timeout`, `retry`, `buildDiscarder`, `disableConcurrentBuilds`, `timestamps`, `skipDefaultCheckout`. `parameters` for build parameters. `triggers` for `cron`/`pollSCM` — prefer SCM webhooks, since polling is a poll loop against your version control server. `when` for conditional stages (`branch`, `changeset`, `expression`, and `beforeAgent true` so you do not provision an agent merely to decide to skip). `post` blocks: `always`, `success`, `failure`, `unstable`, `aborted`, `changed`, `fixed`, `regression`, `unsuccessful`, `cleanup`.

**Agents as containers.** `agent { docker { image 'node:20' args '-v /cache:/cache' } }` runs the stage's steps inside a container on a Docker-capable node, with the workspace bind-mounted so files persist to the node. `agent { kubernetes { yaml ... } }` (Kubernetes plugin) provisions a pod per build with one container per tool plus the JNLP agent container; steps target a container with `container('maven') { sh 'mvn ...' }`. This is the standard modern setup because it makes agents ephemeral and elastic, which cures the classic Jenkins disease of snowflake agents where builds pass on `build-07` and fail on `build-03` for reasons nobody can reconstruct.

**Multibranch pipelines.** A Multibranch Pipeline job scans a repository, finds every branch (and optionally every PR) containing a `Jenkinsfile`, creates a job for each automatically, and deletes them when the branch disappears. This is how you get per-branch CI without hand-creating jobs — the Jenkins expression of pipeline-as-code, with the pipeline definition versioned alongside the source it builds.

sections.title: 7. Jenkins in Production: Shared Libraries, CPS Traps, Credentials, Workspaces
sections.content:
The Jenkinsfile in the previous section is the interview answer. What separates someone who has actually operated Jenkins is knowing where it bites.

**Groovy CPS is not normal Groovy.** Jenkins pipeline code must survive a controller restart mid-build. It achieves this by running your Groovy through a *continuation-passing style* transformer that serialises execution state to disk at every step boundary. Consequences that surprise people: every local variable in flight must be `java.io.Serializable`, so holding a non-serializable object — a `Matcher` from a regex, a parsed JSON node, a file handle — across an `sh` step throws `NotSerializableException`. Some Groovy constructs, notably closures passed to `.each` and some iterator patterns, behave unexpectedly under CPS, which is why the standard advice is to use a plain indexed `for` loop in pipeline code. CPS is also *slow*: it is interpreted, and step boundaries hit disk, so heavy Groovy computation hammers the controller — remember that Groovy in a Jenkinsfile executes on the **controller**, not the agent, even though `sh` steps run on the agent. The fixes: annotate helper methods with `@NonCPS` so they run as ordinary Groovy (they then may not call pipeline steps like `sh` or `echo`), and push real logic out of Groovy into shell scripts or a compiled tool checked into the repo. "The Jenkinsfile orchestrates; it does not compute" is the right instinct.

**Shared libraries.** A Jenkins shared library is a Git repository with a fixed layout: `vars/` holds global variables and steps (a file `vars/buildJavaService.groovy` defining `call(Map cfg)` becomes a step `buildJavaService(...)` in any Jenkinsfile), `src/` holds regular Groovy classes on the classpath, and `resources/` holds non-Groovy files loadable with `libraryResource`. Load it with `@Library('acme-ci@v3') _` at the top of a Jenkinsfile, or configure it as an implicitly-loaded global library. This is the mechanism that lets 200 service repos each carry a five-line Jenkinsfile. The critical operational detail: **pin the library to a tag or commit, not to a floating branch.** `@Library('acme-ci')` resolving to the default branch means one merge instantly changes the behaviour of every pipeline in the company, with no rollout, no canary, and no rollback.

**Credentials.** Jenkins stores credentials encrypted inside `$JENKINS_HOME`, with the master key on the same disk — so treat `$JENKINS_HOME` itself as a secret. Pipelines get them two ways. `environment { FOO = credentials('id') }` binds by type: a secret-text credential yields `FOO`; a **username/password credential yields `FOO`, `FOO_USR`, and `FOO_PSW`** (a detail interviewers genuinely ask about); an SSH key or secret file yields a path to a temporary file. The more disciplined form is `withCredentials([...]) { }`, which scopes the binding to a block so the secret is not in the environment of every subsequent step. Jenkins masks bound credential values in console output, but that masking is a string replace on the log stream — it does not survive base64 encoding, string splitting, or a subprocess writing the value into a file that then gets archived. Two habits follow: never interpolate a secret with Groovy `"${TOKEN}"` (that value is baked into the generated script text and can leak through process listings and logs) — use single-quoted shell strings so the shell expands it from the environment. And prefer holding no long-lived cloud keys in Jenkins at all: exchange a short-lived identity token with the cloud provider, or fetch dynamic credentials from Vault.

**Workspaces and the stateful-agent problem.** An agent's workspace is a real directory that persists between builds on that agent. This is a feature (incremental builds are fast) and a bug factory (a stale `node_modules`, a leftover generated file, a `.git` in a strange state makes a build pass or fail for reasons not present in the source). `cleanWs()` in `post { cleanup }` and a clean-before-checkout SCM extension address it; containerised or Kubernetes agents solve it structurally because the workspace dies with the pod. When you hear "it works on my machine, and on agent 4, but not agent 7," the answer is almost always workspace or agent-image drift.

**Passing files between stages.** Parallel stages and stages with different `agent` directives can land on different machines, so files do not follow automatically. `stash`/`unstash` moves a small file set — but it routes *through the controller*, so stashing a 2 GB build output degrades the whole instance for everyone. `archiveArtifacts` stores outputs permanently against the build record. For anything large, push to an artifact repository or object store and pass the coordinates as a string.

sections.title: 8. GitLab CI: Stages, the needs DAG, rules, and Artifacts vs Cache
sections.content:
GitLab CI is configured by `.gitlab-ci.yml` at the repository root. Its model is jobs plus stages, and the parts interviewers ask about are `rules`, `needs`, and the artifacts/cache distinction.

**Stages and jobs.** You declare an ordered `stages:` list; every job names its `stage:`. All jobs in a stage run in parallel; the next stage starts only when every job in the previous one has succeeded. That is simple and easy to reason about, and it is also a throughput ceiling: a stage takes as long as its slowest job even when a downstream job depended only on a fast one. **`needs:`** breaks the stage barrier and turns the pipeline into a true DAG — a job with `needs: [build]` starts the moment `build` finishes, regardless of what else shares `build`'s stage. `needs: []` starts a job immediately at pipeline start. Adding `needs` to a linear pipeline is usually the single largest wall-clock win available for free.

**Runners and executors.** A GitLab Runner is an agent process that long-polls the GitLab instance for jobs. Its **executor** decides how the job body runs: `shell` (directly on the runner host — fast, and a security disaster on shared runners, since jobs share a filesystem and user), `docker` (each job in a fresh container from the job's `image:`, with `services:` containers such as Postgres or Redis attached on the same network and addressable by alias), `docker-autoscaler`/`docker+machine` (autoscaling ephemeral VMs), and `kubernetes` (a pod per job). Job-to-runner matching is by `tags:`. On self-managed GitLab the most common security mistake mirrors the GitHub one: a shared `shell`-executor runner reachable by every project, where any job can read any other project's checked-out source and leftover credentials.

**`rules` is the modern conditional.** `only`/`except` are legacy; write `rules:` with `if`, `changes`, and `exists`, each optionally setting `when` (`on_success`, `manual`, `always`, `never`, `delayed`) and `allow_failure`. Rules are evaluated top-down and the **first match wins**, so ordering matters and a terminal `- when: never` is the safe default. `workflow: rules:` at the top level decides whether the *pipeline itself* is created — the correct place to stop duplicate pipelines, which is the classic "a branch pipeline and a merge-request pipeline both run for every push" waste that doubles your runner bill.

**Artifacts vs cache — a favourite question.** They are not interchangeable.

- **Artifacts** are job *outputs*. They upload to the GitLab server when the job finishes, are guaranteed available to downstream jobs (by default all jobs in later stages; scoped with `dependencies:` or `needs:artifacts`), are visible and downloadable in the UI, and expire per `expire_in`. Use for build outputs, test reports, coverage, binaries. `artifacts:reports:*` are special-cased and parsed by GitLab — `junit` (test results in the MR widget), `dotenv` (injects variables into downstream jobs), coverage and security report types.
- **Cache** is a *performance optimisation for inputs*. It is stored per runner, or in shared object storage if configured, keyed by `cache:key`, and it is **best-effort**: a job must still be correct when the cache is empty. Use for `node_modules`, `~/.m2`, `.gradle`, pip wheels. `cache:policy: pull` on consumers avoids the upload cost; the single job that populates it uses the default `pull-push`.

The rule of thumb: if a downstream job *breaks* when the thing is missing, it is an artifact. If it merely gets slower, it is a cache. Passing a compiled binary between jobs via cache is a bug that manifests as a mysterious failure the first time the job lands on a different runner.

**Other things worth naming.** `extends:` plus hidden `.template` jobs and YAML anchors for DRY config. `include:` (local, project, remote, template) for cross-repo pipeline sharing, with `include:rules` for conditional inclusion. `parallel: N` to fan a job into N instances exposing `CI_NODE_INDEX`/`CI_NODE_TOTAL` for test sharding, and `parallel:matrix:` for combination builds. `environment:` with `url` and `on_stop` for review apps that spin up per merge request and tear themselves down on merge. `resource_group:` to serialise deployment jobs so two pipelines cannot deploy the same environment concurrently. `retry:` with `when:` so you retry only infrastructure failures (`runner_system_failure`, `stuck_or_timeout_failure`) rather than papering over genuine test flakiness. And `trigger:` for parent-child pipelines — a huge monorepo win, where a parent job *generates* a child `.yml` from the changed paths and triggers it — and for multi-project pipelines.

  npm_config_cache: "$CI_PROJECT_DIR/.npm"   # keep the cache inside the project dir

workflow:                              # stop duplicate branch+MR pipelines
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_TAG'
    - when: never

  cache:

    paths: [.npm/]

    - npm ci --prefer-offline
    - npm run build

sections.title: 9. Caching in CI: Key Design, Correctness, and Why Your Cache Is Lying
sections.content:
CI runners are ephemeral by design, so every job starts cold: no dependency directory, no compiler output, no image layers. Caching buys that back, and it is usually the difference between a four-minute and a fourteen-minute pipeline. It is also the most common source of "CI is broken, but only sometimes," because a cache is mutable global state that your build silently reads.

**The non-negotiable invariant: a cache miss must cost only time, never correctness.** If a job produces a different result warm than cold, the cache is a bug. Test it — run a scheduled pipeline with caching disabled and confirm identical results. The most common violation is caching a *build output* directory (`dist/`, `target/`, `build/`) whose staleness detection relies on file mtimes, which do not survive an archive round-trip cleanly, so an incremental build decides everything is up to date when it is not.

**Key design is the whole game.** A cache entry has a key and, in most systems, a set of fallback prefixes. The key should be a hash of everything the content depends on:

```
key = <os>-<arch>-<toolchain-version>-<hash of lockfile>
```

Hash the *lockfile*, not `package.json` or `pom.xml`, because the lockfile is what determines the resolved dependency tree. In GitHub Actions that is `hashFiles('**/package-lock.json')`; in GitLab it is `cache:key:files:`. Include OS and architecture, because native modules compiled on `ubuntu-22.04` will not load on `macos-14` or on `arm64`, and a cache crossing that boundary produces baffling runtime errors that look like corrupt binaries.

**Restore-keys are a prefix-match fallback, and they are a trade.** `restore-keys: [ npm-linux- ]` means "if the exact key misses, restore the most recent entry whose key starts with this prefix." That turns a cold start into a warm-ish start after a lockfile change — you get most of the packages and download only the deltas. But the restored content does *not* match the current lockfile, so your install step **must** reconcile rather than trust. `npm ci` (which removes `node_modules` and installs exactly the lockfile) is safe; `npm install` against a partially stale tree is exactly where phantom dependency versions come from.

**Cache entries are immutable in GitHub Actions.** Once a key is written it is never overwritten. This surprises people who write `key: deps-${{ runner.os }}` with no hash: the first run populates it and every subsequent run restores that increasingly ancient snapshot forever. If the key does not change when the content should change, you have built a permanent stale cache.

**Scope and poisoning.** In GitHub Actions, caches are scoped by branch: a run can restore caches created on its own ref, on the base branch of its pull request, and on the default branch. A cache written by a topic branch is *not* visible to `main`. That is deliberate — a pull request cannot poison the default branch's cache. But it does mean one workflow can influence another within a branch's scope, so treat cached content as untrusted to the extent untrusted code could have produced it. Never cache credentials, and never cache a directory that a test suite writes into. GitHub also enforces a per-repository cache size limit (10 GB at the time of writing) with LRU eviction and removal of entries unused for 7 days, so an over-eager caching strategy evicts the entries that actually mattered.

**What to cache, ranked by return.** (1) The package manager's *download* cache — `~/.npm`, `~/.m2/repository`, `~/.cache/pip`, `~/go/pkg/mod`, `~/.gradle/caches`. This is the safest and usually the biggest win, because the cached content is immutable content-addressed tarballs and the install step still runs and validates. (2) Docker layer cache, which has its own section. (3) Compiler caches with content-addressed keys — `ccache`, `sccache`, Gradle or Bazel remote build caches — safe by design because they key on input hashes rather than timestamps. (4) `node_modules` itself: faster still, and the riskiest, because it makes install a no-op, so any key error becomes a correctness error.

**The measurement that ends the argument.** Log cache hit rate and time saved. A cache with a 20 percent hit rate that adds 40 seconds of upload on every miss is a net loss. That is a real outcome when the key includes something that changes every run — a timestamp, `github.sha`, `CI_JOB_ID` — producing a write-only cache that is pure overhead and steadily evicting everything useful.

# ---------- GitHub Actions ----------
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  id: npm-cache
  with:
    path: ~/.npm                                   # the DOWNLOAD cache, not node_modules
    key: npm-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
    restore-keys: |
      npm-${{ runner.os }}-
- run: npm ci                                      # reconciles against the lockfile
- run: echo "cache hit = ${{ steps.npm-cache.outputs.cache-hit }}"

# JVM: key on every file that can change dependency resolution
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: |
      ~/.gradle/caches
      ~/.gradle/wrapper
    key: gradle-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/*.gradle*','**/gradle-wrapper.properties') }}
    restore-keys: gradle-${{ runner.os }}-

# ANTI-PATTERNS
#   key: deps-${{ runner.os }}
#     -> never changes; GHA cache entries are immutable; permanently stale.
#   key: deps-${{ github.sha }}
#     -> changes every run; ~0% hit rate; pure upload overhead + evicts good entries.
#   path: node_modules   with   run: npm install
#     -> stale tree + partial install = phantom versions that reproduce nowhere.
#   caching a directory the test suite writes into
#     -> one job's leftovers silently become the next job's inputs.

# ---------- GitLab ----------
cache:
  key:
    files: [package-lock.json]      # GitLab hashes the listed file(s) for you
    prefix: ${CI_JOB_IMAGE}         # keep node:18 and node:20 caches apart
  paths: [.npm/]
  policy: pull                      # consumers pull; one producer uses pull-push

# ---------- verify the invariant on a schedule ----------
# A nightly pipeline with caching disabled. If its results differ from the
# cached pipeline's, the cache is a correctness bug, not a speedup.

sections.title: 10. Container Builds in CI: Layers, BuildKit, and Cache Backends
sections.content:
For most teams the slowest thing in the pipeline is `docker build`, and the reason is almost always a misunderstanding of the layer cache.

**The mechanism.** A Docker image is an ordered stack of read-only layers, each the filesystem diff produced by one instruction. During a build, the builder computes a cache key for each instruction from the parent layer's identity plus the instruction itself; for `COPY`/`ADD` the key also includes a checksum of the copied files' contents and metadata. If the key matches an existing layer, that layer is reused and the instruction is not executed. Crucially, **the cache invalidates transitively**: the moment one instruction misses, every instruction after it rebuilds, because their parent identity has changed.

That single fact dictates Dockerfile ordering. Put the instructions that change least at the top and the ones that change every commit at the bottom. The canonical mistake is:

```
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
```

Here `COPY . .` includes your source, which changes on every commit, so `npm ci` re-runs on every commit and downloads the entire dependency tree again. The fix is to copy only the dependency manifest first:

```
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
```

Now `npm ci` is cached until the lockfile actually changes. The same shape applies to `go.mod`/`go.sum`, `pom.xml`, `requirements.txt`, `Cargo.toml`. Add a `.dockerignore` that excludes `.git`, `node_modules`, and build outputs — without it, the build context upload alone can take a minute and any local `node_modules` change busts `COPY . .`.

**Multi-stage builds** separate the build environment from the runtime image. A `FROM ... AS build` stage holds compilers, dev dependencies, and test tooling; a second, minimal `FROM` stage copies only the produced artifacts. This is both a size win (a Go binary in a distroless image is tens of megabytes rather than a gigabyte) and a security win — your production image cannot be exploited via a compiler, a package manager, or a shell it does not contain. BuildKit also builds independent stages concurrently.

**BuildKit** is the modern builder (default in current Docker, and what `docker buildx` drives). Three features matter in CI. `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm` gives a persistent cache directory that lives *outside* the image layers, so the package manager's download cache survives across builds without bloating the image and without being invalidated by an unrelated layer change. `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc` mounts a secret into a single `RUN` step's filesystem so it is never written into a layer — solving the classic leak where an `ARG NPM_TOKEN` remains readable forever in the image history. And `--cache-from`/`--cache-to` let you export the layer cache to somewhere durable.

**The ephemeral-runner problem.** A fresh runner has an empty local layer cache, so none of the above helps unless the cache is *imported*. Options, roughly in order of preference: `--cache-to type=registry,ref=...,mode=max` pushes the cache to your registry as a separate artifact and `--cache-from type=registry,ref=...` pulls it — durable, shared across runners, and `mode=max` also exports intermediate stage layers (important for multi-stage builds). On GitHub Actions, `type=gha` uses the Actions cache service instead. `type=local` writes to a directory you then cache with your CI's own cache mechanism, which requires care to avoid unbounded growth. And on self-hosted or Kubernetes runners you can run a persistent BuildKit daemon that keeps a warm local cache for all builds — the fastest option, at the cost of a stateful shared component that is now a trust boundary.

**Multi-arch.** `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64` builds both and pushes a manifest list. Under the hood that means either QEMU emulation on one machine (correct but slow — cross-compiled languages should instead build natively and only cross-package) or a builder with native nodes of each architecture. If your production fleet is Graviton or Ampere and your CI runners are x86, this is not optional, and forgetting it produces an image that pulls fine and then crash-loops with `exec format error`.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# ---------- layer-ordering matters more than any flag ----------
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./         # changes rarely
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc \
    npm ci                                     # cached until the lockfile changes
                                               # the token is never in a layer

FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .                                       # changes every commit -> last
RUN npm run build

FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=deps  /app/node_modules ./node_modules
USER 1000
CMD ["dist/server.js"]

# ---------- .dockerignore (do not skip this) ----------
# .git
# node_modules
# dist
# **/*.test.ts

# ---------- CI: import/export the layer cache so ephemeral runners stay fast ----
docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc \
  --cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/api:buildcache \
  --cache-to   type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/api:buildcache,mode=max \
  --tag ghcr.io/acme/api:$GIT_SHA \
  --push .

# GitHub Actions variant (uses the Actions cache service instead of a registry):
- uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
- uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
  with:
    push: true
    tags: ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ github.sha }}
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

# ---------- proving where the time goes ----------
docker buildx build --progress=plain .   # per-step timings; CACHED lines are free
docker history ghcr.io/acme/api:$GIT_SHA # layer sizes: find the 800MB apt layer

sections.title: 11. Matrix Builds, Parallelism, Sharding, and the Flaky-Test Tax
sections.content:
Two different problems get solved by "run things in parallel," and interviewers notice when a candidate conflates them.

**A matrix build is about coverage.** You need to know your library works on Node 18, 20, and 22, on Linux, macOS, and Windows, against Postgres 14 and 16. A matrix is a cross-product: the CI system instantiates the job template once per combination and runs each on its own runner. Every instance runs the *same tests* against a *different environment*. In GitHub Actions this is `strategy.matrix` with optional `include` (add a combination, or add extra variables to existing ones) and `exclude` (remove combinations that make no sense, like macOS + Postgres-in-Docker). Two options matter operationally: `fail-fast: true` is the default and cancels all in-flight matrix legs as soon as one fails, which is right when you just want a red/green answer and wrong when you want the full compatibility picture — set `fail-fast: false` for release matrices. `max-parallel` throttles the fan-out so a 40-cell matrix does not consume your entire concurrency quota and starve every other pipeline in the org. In GitLab the equivalent is `parallel:matrix:`; in declarative Jenkins it is the `matrix` directive with `axes` and `excludes`.

**Sharding is about wall-clock time.** You have one environment and 8,000 tests taking 40 minutes. You split the *test set* across N runners so each runs 1/N of it. GitLab gives you `parallel: N` with `CI_NODE_INDEX`/`CI_NODE_TOTAL`; GitHub Actions gives you a matrix over shard indices; Jest, pytest-xdist, Go's package-level parallelism, and most modern runners have native shard flags. The naive split — deal tests round-robin by filename — gives poor balance because test durations follow a long tail: one shard finishes in four minutes and another in twenty, so your wall-clock is still twenty. The fix is **timing-based partitioning**: persist per-test durations from previous runs as an artifact, then greedily bin-pack tests into shards of roughly equal predicted duration. That usually turns a 20-minute worst shard into an 11-minute one with the same runner count.

Both approaches hit the same ceiling: **fan-out has fixed overhead per job**. Each runner must boot, check out the repo, restore caches, and install dependencies — often 60 to 120 seconds. Sharding a 10-minute suite across 20 runners does not produce a 30-second pipeline; it produces roughly 90 seconds of setup plus 30 seconds of tests, 20 times over, at 20 times the compute cost. Compute the crossover point before adding shards, and reduce the per-job setup cost (better caching, prebuilt runner images, a container image with dependencies baked in) before adding parallelism.

**The flaky-test tax.** A flaky test is one that passes and fails on the same commit. Its cost is not the retry time; it is the destruction of the pipeline's meaning. Once a team learns that red might mean nothing, they re-run instead of investigating, and the first *real* failure gets re-run too and merged. The math is brutal: if each test has a 0.1 percent independent flake rate, a 2,000-test suite fails spuriously about 86 percent of the time. At that point your pipeline is a random number generator.

The operational response has three parts. First, **measure** — record every test's pass/fail across runs on the same commit and compute a flake rate per test; a test that has flipped without a code change is flaky by definition. Second, **quarantine**: move known-flaky tests to a non-blocking job that still runs and reports, so the signal is preserved while the gate is unblocked, and put a hard expiry on quarantine so the list cannot grow forever. Third, **fix the causes**, which are boringly repetitive: `sleep`-based waits instead of waiting for a condition, shared mutable state between tests, real clocks, real network calls, ordering dependence (run the suite in random order to expose it), and unclosed database transactions leaking between cases.

A related discipline: **retry only what is safe to retry**. Blanket `retry: 2` on a job hides real flakiness and doubles your worst-case pipeline time. Retry infrastructure failures — runner died, registry timed out, network blip — and let assertion failures fail. GitLab expresses this precisely with `retry:when:`; on GitHub Actions you implement it in the step by inspecting the failure or by scoping retries to the specific network-bound command.
